```{r fit-chart}
            data.frame(date = ff$date, target = ff$target, series = "Fitted", value = ff$fitted))
ggplot(fl, aes(date, value, colour = series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.55) +
  facet_wrap(~ target, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Actual = ink[["muted"]], Fitted = ent_col[["NGFB"]])) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

# Is ARDL the right tool? {#is-ardl-the-right-tool}

```{r mc-setup}
#| include: false
cw <- MC$cw; bnd <- MC$bounds; dyn <- MC$dynamics; asy <- MC$asym; icx <- MC$ic
cvr <- MC$convex_reg; cvs <- MC$convex
n_cw <- sum(cw$ph < 0.10); n_cw5 <- sum(cw$ph < 0.05)
fam_cw <- stats::aggregate(ph ~ family, cw, function(p) mean(p < 0.10))
dw <- function(k, v) stats::setNames(dyn[[v]][dyn$registry == k], dyn$target[dyn$registry == k])
dep_t <- c("c_current", "c_savings", "c_call", "c_fixed_notice", "c_ncd")
dep_lab <- c(c_current = "Current accounts", c_savings = "Savings", c_call = "Call", c_fixed_notice = "Fixed and notice",
             c_ncd = "NCDs")
guard(all(dw("ardl11", "bt_mean")[dep_t] < dw("restricted", "bt_mean")[dep_t]) &&
      all(dw("ardl11", "rmse_oos")[dep_t] < dw("restricted", "rmse_oos")[dep_t]),
      "the ARDL(1,1) form improves every deposit cost on both tests")
kink_t <- cvs$t_kink[cvs$variant == "kink"]
guard(all(kink_t < -3), "the contraction kink is strongly significant in sample")
lin_slope <- cvs$b_gdp[cvs$variant == "linear"][1]; kink_slope <- cvs$b_gdp[cvs$variant == "kink"][1]
guard(abs(kink_slope) < abs(lin_slope) / 5, "with the kink, growth above zero barely moves losses")
pr_t <- cw$ph[cw$family == "pricing"]; names(pr_t) <- cw$target[cw$family == "pricing"]
guard(all(pr_t[setdiff(names(pr_t), c("s_cards", "s_overdrafts"))] < 0.05) && all(pr_t[c("s_cards", "s_overdrafts")] > 0.10),
      "pricing Clark-West claims")
guard(all(cw$ph[cw$target %in% c("clr", "nir_assets", "opex_assets")] > 0.10), "credit and fee/cost models not significant")
guard(all(bnd$decision_asym[bnd$target %in% c("c_savings", "c_call", "c_fixed_notice")] == "no level relationship") &&
      all(bnd$decision[bnd$target %in% c("c_savings", "c_call", "c_fixed_notice")] == "no level relationship"),
      "no level relationship for savings, call and fixed, with or without asymmetry")
guard(dw("asym", "rmse_oos")[["c_current"]] < dw("ardl11", "rmse_oos")[["c_current"]] &&
      dw("asym", "bt_mean")[["c_current"]] > dw("ardl11", "bt_mean")[["c_current"]], "current accounts: asymmetry helps short, hurts long")
cm <- satellite_bma_summary(S1$sats$s_cards)
guard(cm$long_run[cm$driver == "d_repo_pos"] < 0 && cm$pip[cm$driver == "d_repo_pos"] > 0.5 &&
      cm$pip[cm$driver == "d_repo_neg"] < 0.5, "card yields lag rises, follow cuts")
guard(MC$convex_reg$rmse_oos[MC$convex_reg$registry == "kink"] < MC$convex_reg$rmse_oos[MC$convex_reg$registry == "linear"] &&
      sum(unlist(MC$convex_reg[MC$convex_reg$registry == "kink", c("bt_2019", "bt_2021")])) >
      sum(unlist(MC$convex_reg[MC$convex_reg$registry == "linear", c("bt_2019", "bt_2021")])), "convex registry claims")
```

The question deserves a direct answer, and it has three parts: why an ARDL
is a sensible core for this problem, what alternatives and refinements could
do better, and what happened when the most promising of them were tested on
the same footing as the satellites themselves.

## Why ARDL

* **Scenarios are conditional forecasts.** A scenario fixes the macro path;
  the models must say what the industry does *given* that path. Single-equation
  models conditioned on exogenous drivers do exactly that. A VAR would model
  the macro variables too, which a scenario overrides anyway.
* **Seventy quarters is a small sample.** An AR(1) term plus at most three
  drivers is about as much structure as 2008–2025 can support, and the sign
  restrictions stop the search from fitting noise with economically wrong
  coefficients.
* **The long run is interpretable.** An ARDL in levels is an error-correction
  model in disguise: $\beta/(1-\rho)$ is the steady-state effect of a driver,
  which is what a three-year projection converges to.
* **It is the supervisors' workhorse.** The Federal Reserve models 20 of the 24
  core components of pre-provision net revenue in its supervisory stress test
  with autoregressive models of ratios, and ECB research argues for averaging
  over many satellite equations rather than hand-picking one (Gross and
  Población, 2015), which is what the model averaging here does.

## What could do better, and what was tested

```{r mc-table}
#| echo: false
tested <- data.frame(
  Refinement = c("Out-of-sample significance (Clark–West)", "Level relationship (Pesaran–Shin–Smith bounds test)",
                 "Impact and long-run pass-through estimated separately (ARDL(1,1) for deposit costs)",
                 "Asymmetric pass-through of hikes and cuts (partial sums)",
                 "Convex credit losses (a kink in GDP growth below zero; log credit-loss ratio)",
                 "Intercept correction at every origin; as a level shift or in the equation",
                 "Forecast combination: BIC weights against the five best out of sample, and the single best"),
  Question = c("Do the satellites beat an AR(1) by more than chance?", "Is a deposit cost tied to the repo rate in the long run?",
               "Does a richer short-run response forecast better?", "Do hikes and cuts pass through differently?",
               "Do losses rise faster in a contraction than they fall in a boom?",
               "Does the correction help, and in which form?", "Is model averaging the right way to use the search?"),
  Verdict = c(sprintf("%d of %d at 10%% (h = %d); pricing strongest, credit and fees/costs not significant", n_cw, nrow(cw), CFG$h_oos),
              sprintf("confirmed for current accounts only; none for savings, call or fixed deposits"),
              "adopted: better for all five deposit costs, on both tests",
              sprintf("significant in sample for %d of %d pricing targets; adopted for savings deposits and card yields", sum(asy$p_sym < 0.10), nrow(asy)),
              "strong in sample, better at 1–4 quarters, worse in the back-test: kept as a scenario sensitivity",
              "adopted as a level shift; helps fees and deposit costs, not credit losses",
              "BIC model averaging kept: it beat both alternatives in the back-test"),
  check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
kt(tested, align = "lll", caption = "Refinements tested in analysis/08_model_checks.R. Every test uses dynamic forecasts conditional on the realised macro path: pseudo-out-of-sample from expanding windows (horizons 1–4) and the eight-quarter back-test from 2019Q4 and 2021Q4.")
```

The rule for adopting a refinement was fixed before looking at the scenario
results: it enters the core only if it improves **both** the pseudo-out-of-sample
fit of the selected specification and the eight-quarter back-test of the
model-averaged projection, the way the scenarios use it. Anything that passes
one test and fails the other is reported as a sensitivity, not adopted.

### Do the satellites beat the AR(1) by more than chance?

With some 4,000 specifications searched per target, a winning specification
can beat the benchmark by luck. The Clark–West test asks whether the
out-of-sample improvement is larger than the noise a bigger model adds when
its extra coefficients are truly zero (a plain Diebold–Mariano test is biased
against the larger model when the models are nested).

```{r mc-cw}
#| echo: false
cwt <- cw[order(match(cw$family, c("pricing", "credit", "pnl", "volume")), cw$ph), ]
kt(data.frame(Target = S1$summary$label[match(cwt$target, S1$summary$target)], Family = cwt$family,
              `Skill vs AR(1)` = pct(cwt$skill, 0), `Clark-West p, h = 1` = num(cwt$p1, 3),
              `Clark-West p, h = 4` = num(cwt$ph, 3), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "llrrr", caption = sprintf("One-sided p-values; %d expanding-window origins per target. With %d tests at 10%%, about %.0f would pass by chance.",
                                      median(cw$origins), nrow(cw), 0.1 * nrow(cw)))
```

`r n_cw` of `r nrow(cw)` satellites pass at 10% (`r n_cw5` at 5%), far more than
the `r round(0.1 * nrow(cw))` chance alone would deliver. The split by family is
the honest part: every pricing model except cards and overdrafts carries
significant information, the volume models mostly marginal information, and
the credit-loss and fee and cost models do **not** beat the AR(1) significantly
at the four-quarter horizon. For credit losses that is a statement about
2015–2025, which held one deep recession (2020) for the test to score; it is
also why the credit model's economics (losses rise when growth falls) rest on
the full sample and on the model average rather than on its forecasting record.

### Is a deposit cost tied to the repo rate in the long run?

A levels regression of one persistent series on another can be spurious. The
Pesaran–Shin–Smith bounds test asks whether a level relationship exists
without having to know whether the series are stationary; its critical values
are simulated here for the actual sample size.

```{r mc-bounds}
#| echo: false
kt(data.frame(`Deposit cost` = dep_lab[bnd$target], F = num(bnd$F, 2),
              `5% bounds, I(0) / I(1)` = paste(num(bnd$i0_95, 2), "/", num(bnd$i1_95, 2)),
              Decision = bnd$decision, `F, asymmetric` = num(bnd$F_asym, 2),
              `5% bounds, asymmetric` = paste(num(bnd$i0_95_asym, 2), "/", num(bnd$i1_95_asym, 2)),
              `Decision, asymmetric` = bnd$decision_asym, check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lrrlrrl", caption = "Bounds test, unrestricted intercept and no trend, one lag of the differences, impulse dummies as controls. Critical values from 4,000 simulations at the sample size. 'Asymmetric': the repo rate split into cumulative hikes and cuts.")
```

The test confirms a long-run anchor for current accounts and cannot find one
for savings, call and fixed deposits, with or without asymmetry. Part of that
is low power in `r bnd$n[1]` quarters; part is real: the composition of each
BA120 category drifts (digital banks' savings products, the mix of
corporate and retail call money), so the level relationship moves. The
practical consequence is that these deposit costs are best modelled through
their short-run response to rate *changes*, which is well identified, with a
long run that is pinned down weakly, and that is what the next refinement does.

### Impact and long-run pass-through, and asymmetry

The original search allowed the repo level *or* its change in a deposit-cost
equation, never both. That forces the impact of a rate move and its long-run
pass-through into one geometric profile. Letting both enter (an ARDL(1,1))
separates them:

```{r mc-dyn}
#| echo: false
dt <- data.frame(`Deposit cost` = dep_lab[dep_t],
                 `OOS RMSE: original` = num(dw("restricted", "rmse_oos")[dep_t], 3),
                 `ARDL(1,1)` = num(dw("ardl11", "rmse_oos")[dep_t], 3),
                 `ARDL(1,1), asymmetric` = num(dw("asym", "rmse_oos")[dep_t], 3),
                 `Back-test RMSE: original` = num(dw("restricted", "bt_mean")[dep_t], 3),
                 `ARDL(1,1) ` = num(dw("ardl11", "bt_mean")[dep_t], 3),
                 `ARDL(1,1), asymmetric ` = num(dw("asym", "bt_mean")[dep_t], 3),
                 `Symmetry rejected (p)` = num(asy$p_sym[match(dep_t, asy$target)], 3),
                 Adopted = ifelse(dep_t %in% asy$target[asy$adopt], "ARDL(1,1), asymmetric", "ARDL(1,1)"),
                 check.names = FALSE)
kt(dt, align = "lrrrrrrrl", caption = "Deposit-cost models under three registries. OOS RMSE: the selected specification, horizons 1–4. Back-test RMSE: the model-averaged projection over eight quarters, mean of the 2019Q4 and 2021Q4 origins (percentage points). Symmetry test: HAC Wald test of equal pass-through of hikes and cuts, nested in the ARDL(1,1).")
```

The ARDL(1,1) improves all five deposit costs on both tests and is adopted.
Asymmetry is significant in sample for `r sum(asy$p_sym[asy$target %in% dep_t] < 0.10)` of the five,
but among deposit costs it improves both forecast tests only for savings
deposits, where hikes pass through more than cuts (the back-test error falls from
`r num(dw("ardl11", "bt_mean")[["c_savings"]], 2)` to `r num(dw("asym", "bt_mean")[["c_savings"]], 2)`
percentage points); for current accounts it helps at one to four quarters but
hurts over eight. The partial sums trend, so a model that uses them can drift
when projected far from the sample, which is why the rule's second test matters.
Among the loan spreads over prime, splitting the change in the repo rate into
rises and falls improves both tests only for credit cards (back-test error
`r num(dw("ardl11", "bt_mean")[["s_cards"]], 2)` against `r num(dw("asym", "bt_mean")[["s_cards"]], 2)`), where it is adopted:
card yields fall behind prime when rates rise but follow it down when rates
fall.

### Are credit losses convex in a contraction?

```{r mc-convex}
#| echo: false
na_dash <- function(x) ifelse(grepl("NA", x), "—", x)
kt(data.frame(`Base specification` = cvs$base, Variant = cvs$variant,
              `GDP slope` = num(cvs$b_gdp, 3), `Kink slope (growth below 0)` = na_dash(num(cvs$b_kink, 3)),
              `t, kink` = na_dash(num(cvs$t_kink, 1)), `OOS RMSE` = num(cvs$rmse_oos, 3),
              `Back-test RMSE, 2019Q4` = num(cvs$rmse_bt_2019, 3), `Back-test RMSE, 2021Q4` = num(cvs$rmse_bt_2021, 3),
              check.names = FALSE),
   align = "llrrrrrr", caption = "Credit-loss ratio: the two leading members of the model average, linear, with a kink in GDP growth below zero, and in logs. Log-model slopes are semi-elasticities.")
```

The data say yes, strongly in sample: with a kink, growth above zero barely
moves the loss ratio (slope `r num(kink_slope, 3)` against `r num(lin_slope, 3)` in the
linear model) while each point of contraction adds `r num(-cvs$b_kink[cvs$variant == "kink"][1], 3)` pp
on impact ($t$ = `r num(kink_t[1], 1)`). The kinked model also forecasts
better at one to four quarters (RMSE `r num(cvr$rmse_oos[cvr$registry == "kink"], 3)` against
`r num(cvr$rmse_oos[cvr$registry == "linear"], 3)` for the full search), but not over the
eight-quarter back-test, where it has only 2009 to learn the kink from before
2020. It is therefore a sensitivity rather than the core, and an important
one, shown in [Scenarios](#scenarios): it removes about
`r pct((mr["upside", "core"] - mr["upside", "convex"]) / att_r("upside", "NGFB", "credit"), 0)` of the upside's
credit benefit and leaves the downside almost unchanged.

### The intercept correction

```{r mc-ic}
#| echo: false
ict <- icx[order(match(icx$family, c("credit", "pnl", "pricing")), icx$target), ]
kt(data.frame(Target = S1$summary$label[match(ict$target, S1$summary$target)], AR = num(ict$rho, 2),
              `RMSE, no correction` = num(ict$rmse_no_ic, 3), `RMSE ratio, level shift` = num(ict$ratio, 2),
              `RMSE ratio, in the equation` = num(ict$ratio_equation, 2), `Diebold-Mariano p (level)` = num(ict$p, 3),
              check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lrrrrr", caption = "The correction (mean residual of the last four unflagged quarters) evaluated at every pseudo-out-of-sample origin. Ratios below one favour the correction. AR: the autoregressive coefficient of the selected model.")
```

The previous version added the recent residual to the equation's intercept,
where it compounds through the autoregressive term to roughly
$\text{ic}/(1-\rho)$. That is the right correction for a shift in a series'
equilibrium mean, but with the ARDL(1,1) deposit models, whose $\rho$ is close
to one, it turns a few basis points of recent residual into a drift of a
percentage point or more. Applied instead as a level shift of the projected
path, the correction helps non-interest revenue (RMSE
`r pct(1 - ict$ratio[ict$target == "nir_assets"], 0)` lower), current, call and fixed
deposits and the overdraft and term-loan spreads, and is neutral or slightly
negative elsewhere.
It does not help the credit-loss ratio, where it lowers the projected loss
ratio by about `r num(100 * (mr["baseline", "no_ic_credit_clr"] - mr["baseline", "core_clr"]), 2)` pp of
loans and is worth `r ubps(mr["baseline", "core"] - mr["baseline", "no_ic_credit"])` of NGFB's
baseline ROE: the single largest modelling assumption behind the *level* of
ROE in this report (the two-origin back-test favours it; the test across
`r cw$origins[cw$target == "clr"]` origins slightly disfavours it, not significantly).

### Model averaging, selection or combination?

```{r mc-comb}
#| echo: false
cb <- MC$comb
kt(data.frame(Family = cb$family, `BIC model average (used)` = pct(cb$skill_used, 0),
              `Five best out of sample, equal weights` = pct(cb$skill_comb, 0),
              `Single best out of sample` = pct(cb$skill_best, 0), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lrrr", caption = "Median back-test skill against no change, with the whole search re-run at each origin.")
```

Selecting the specification with the best pseudo-out-of-sample record is the
natural instinct, and it is wrong here: on genuinely new data the single best
specification does worst (median skill `r pct(MC$comb_all[["best"]], 0)`), an equal-weighted
average of the five best does little better (`r pct(MC$comb_all[["comb"]], 0)`), and the
BIC-weighted model average does best (`r pct(MC$comb_all[["bma"]], 0)`). Ranking by
out-of-sample RMSE over a few dozen origins overfits the ranking itself (a
winner's curse), while BIC weights spread the bet across specifications that
fit the whole sample.

## What would improve accuracy most

The tests point to the data rather than the model class. In order of likely
value:

1. **A bank's own data.** NGFB inherits the sector's pricing and loss rates.
   A real bank would replace the Stage 1 pricing with its own product pricing
   and the relative loss multipliers with its own loss history, which removes
   the largest source of error at bank level.
2. **Monthly data for pricing -- tested, and it does not.** BA120 is monthly
   (`r nrow(P$spnl) * 3` months against `r nrow(P$spnl)` quarters), so estimating the pricing
   models monthly looked like the obvious way to sharpen the short-run
   dynamics the tests above found to matter. The [next chapter](#monthly) does
   it, and the monthly models forecast the same quarterly outcomes less
   accurately: the extra observations bring more noise than information about
   repricing that happens over quarters.
3. **Loss data by product.** BA200 publishes no losses by product, so credit
   enters the engine as one sector ratio with assumed relative multipliers;
   impairment data by asset class would allow a product-level credit model,
   and a convex one with more than two recessions to learn from.
4. **Longer samples through structural breaks.** IFRS 9 (2018) changed how
   losses are recognised; a time-varying intercept (a state-space local
   level) is the principled version of the intercept correction once there
   is enough post-2018 data to estimate it.

Machine-learning alternatives are a poor fit for this problem: with 70
observations they overfit, and tree-based methods cannot extrapolate beyond the
historical range, which a downside scenario routinely requires.

# Monthly frequency: would the models fit better? {#monthly}

```{r m-setup}
#| include: false
MM <- rd("monthly.rds"); DY <- rd("dynamics.rds")
tdg <- MM$disaggregation$gdp
nc <- MM$nowcast
ncv <- function(ind, mod, col) nc[nc$indicators == ind & nc$model == mod, col]
best_nc <- nc[nc$indicators == "coinc + mfg + retail" & nc$model == "chow-lin", ]
guard(best_nc$rmse_ex2020 == min(nc$rmse_ex2020) && best_nc$rmse_ex2020 < best_nc$rmse_ar1_ex2020,
      "the chosen GDP disaggregation is the best nowcaster and beats the AR(1)")
guard(ncv("none", "litterman", "rmse_ex2020") > best_nc$rmse_ar1_ex2020, "without indicators the monthly path adds nothing")
rc <- MM$race
rw <- stats::reshape(rc[, c("target", "family", "block", "model", "rmse")], idvar = c("target", "family", "block"),
                     timevar = "model", direction = "wide")
names(rw) <- sub("^rmse\\.", "", names(rw))
models <- c("q_ardl", "q_pdl", "q_shrink", "q_ar1", "m_ardl", "m_pdl", "m_shrink", "m_ar1")
for (k in models[-1]) rw[[paste0("r_", k)]] <- rw[[k]] / rw$q_ardl
## (a model class with no admissible specification for a target drops out of that median)
med <- function(fam, k, b) stats::median(rw[[paste0("r_", k)]][rw$family %in% fam & rw$block == b], na.rm = TRUE)
fam_lab <- c(volume = "Volumes", pricing = "Pricing", credit = "Credit losses", pnl = "Fees and costs")
dm <- MM$dm
n_q_better <- sum(dm$p_value < 0.10 & dm$dm_stat < 0); n_m_better <- sum(dm$p_value < 0.10 & dm$dm_stat > 0)
no_pdl_q <- unique(rw$target[is.na(rw$q_pdl)]); no_pdl_m <- unique(rw$target[is.na(rw$m_pdl)])
guard(length(no_pdl_m) == 0 && all(no_pdl_q %in% c("g_mortgages_res")), "PDL coverage note")
rwt <- function(t, col, b = "h1_4") rw[rw$target == t & rw$block == b, col]
dmv <- function(t, col) dm[dm$target == t, col]
## the two lumpy books that monthly models forecast better
lumpy <- c("g_corp_all", "g_beh_term")
guard(MM$vol_source == "BA900" && all(dm$dm_stat[dm$target %in% lumpy] > 0 & dm$p_value[dm$target %in% lumpy] < 0.01) &&
        all(vapply(lumpy, function(t) rwt(t, "r_m_ardl") < 0.9 && rwt(t, "r_m_ardl", "h5_8") < 0.9 &&
                     rwt(t, "r_m_ar1") < min(1, rwt(t, "r_q_ar1")), TRUE)) &&
        n_m_better == length(lumpy) && all(dm$target[dm$p_value < 0.10 & dm$dm_stat > 0] %in% lumpy),
      "corporate loans and term deposits: significantly better monthly, through the dynamics")
guard(med("volume", "m_ar1", "h1_4") < med("volume", "q_ar1", "h1_4"), "monthly AR(1) is the best volume forecaster")
lag1_m <- vapply(lumpy, function(t) { x <- MM$panel_m[[t]][MM$panel_m$date >= MM$m_args$sample_from]
  x <- x[is.finite(x)]; stats::cor(x[-1], x[-length(x)]) }, 0)
guard(all(lag1_m < 0), "lumpy books: month-to-month growth reverses")
## robustness: the monthly models on their own definition of the quarterly P&L outcome
ro <- stats::reshape(MM$race_own[, c("target", "family", "block", "model", "rmse")], idvar = c("target", "family", "block"),
                     timevar = "model", direction = "wide")
ro$r <- ro$rmse.m_ardl / ro$rmse.q_ardl
med_own <- function(fam, b) stats::median(ro$r[ro$family %in% fam & ro$block == b])
guard(med_own("pricing", "h1_4") > 1.1 && med_own("pricing", "h5_8") > 1.1, "pricing: monthly is worse on its own definition too")
dg <- MM$def_gap; dgv <- function(t, col) dg[dg$target == t, col]
guard(MM$pnl_source == "BA120 and BA100 monthly" && dgv("c_savings", "mean_abs_gap") < 0.05 &&
        max(dgv("c_current", "max_abs_gap"), dgv("c_ncd", "max_abs_gap")) > 0.3 &&
        all(format(c(dgv("c_current", "max_date"), dgv("c_ncd", "max_date")), "%Y") %in% c("2008", "2009")),
      "definition-gap note")
guard(med("pricing", "m_ardl", "h1_4") > 1.1 && med("pricing", "m_ardl", "h5_8") > 1.1, "monthly pricing models are worse")
guard(med("volume", "m_ardl", "h1_4") > 1 && med("volume", "m_ardl", "h5_8") > 1, "monthly volume models are worse")
guard(med("credit", "m_ardl", "h1_4") < 1, "monthly credit-loss model is better at short horizons")
guard(n_q_better > n_m_better, "more significant differences favour the quarterly models")
guard(med("pricing", "q_pdl", "h1_4") > 1 && med("pricing", "q_shrink", "h1_4") > 1 &&
        med("pricing", "m_pdl", "h1_4") > med("pricing", "m_ardl", "h1_4") &&
        med("pricing", "m_shrink", "h1_4") > med("pricing", "m_ardl", "h1_4"),
      "ARDL beats PDL and shrinkage in pricing at both frequencies")
guard(med("volume", "q_ar1", "h1_4") < 1 && med("volume", "q_ar1", "h5_8") < 1, "the AR(1) beats macro models for volumes at short horizons")
guard(all(vapply(c("q_pdl", "q_shrink", "m_ardl", "m_pdl", "m_shrink"), function(k)
  med("volume", k, "h1_4") > med("volume", "q_ar1", "h1_4"), TRUE)), "no macro model beats the AR(1) for volumes")
guard(all(dm$p_value[dm$target %in% c("clr", "opex_assets")] > 0.10) && med("pnl", "m_ardl", "h5_8") < 1,
      "monthly credit and cost gains are not significant")
sgc <- DY$sign_check
sgv <- function(t, col) sgc[sgc$target == t, col]
guard(sgv("g_mortgages_res", "wrong_weight_free") > 0.99 && sgv("g_mortgages_res", "rmse_free") > 1.2 * sgv("g_mortgages_res", "rmse_restricted"),
      "home loans: without signs, all weight on wrong signs and worse accuracy")
guard(all(sgc$wrong_weight_free[sgc$family == "pricing"] < 0.1), "pricing models agree with the signs")
guard(sgv("clr", "wrong_weight_free") > 0.99 && sgv("clr", "rmse_free") < sgv("clr", "rmse_restricted"),
      "credit losses: the free model is more accurate but wrong-signed")
mu <- DY$multipliers
mval <- function(t, sh, q, st = "production", col = "effect")
  mu[mu$target == t & mu$shock == sh & mu$set == st & abs(mu$quarters - q) < 1e-9, col]
## short panel labels for the multiplier charts
tlab <- c(c_current = "Current accounts", c_savings = "Savings deposits", c_call = "Call deposits",
          c_fixed_notice = "Fixed & notice deposits", c_ncd = "NCDs", s_homeloans = "Home-loan spread",
          s_vaf = "VAF spread", s_cards = "Card spread", stats::setNames(plab, paste0("g_", names(plab))))

guard(all(reg1$g_cards$signs[c("repo", "d_repo", "d4_repo")] == 0) &&

        mval("g_corp_all", "repo_up", 12, col = "lo") < 0 && mval("g_corp_all", "repo_up", 12, col = "hi") > 0,
      "corporate loans: an early rise, a later fall, and a band that spans zero")
gdp_w <- function(t) { b <- S1$sats[[t]]$bma; sum(b$weights[vapply(b$specs, function(s) "gdp_yy" %in% s$d, TRUE)]) }
hpi_w <- function(t) { b <- S1$sats[[t]]$bma; sum(b$weights[vapply(b$specs, function(s) "hpi_yy" %in% s$d, TRUE)]) }
guard(gdp_w("g_mortgages_res") < 0.02 && hpi_w("g_mortgages_res") > 0.2 && abs(mval("g_mortgages_res", "gdp_down", 12)) < 0.01,
      "home loans: no direct GDP channel to speak of; house prices carry it")
## the home-loan lag example
lagw <- function(t, d) {
  b <- S1$sats[[t]]$bma; w <- stats::setNames(numeric(5), 0:4)
  for (i in seq_along(b$specs)) {
    k <- which(b$specs[[i]]$d == d)
    if (length(k)) w[as.character(b$specs[[i]]$l[k])] <- w[as.character(b$specs[[i]]$l[k])] + b$weights[i]
  }
  w
}
hl_d4 <- lagw("g_mortgages_res", "d4_repo")

guard(sum(hl_d4) > 0.6 && all(hl_d4[c("2", "3", "4")] > 0.1) && hl_rate_early <= 0.05 &&

      "home-loan lag example")

guard(mval("c_savings", "repo_up", 12) - abs(mval("c_savings", "repo_down", 12)) > 0.1, "savings: hikes pass through more than cuts")
guard(all(vapply(c("g_mortgages_res", "g_vaf", "g_cards", "g_personal_other"), function(t) mval(t, "repo_up", 12) < 0, TRUE)),
      "loan volumes fall after a hike")
guard(mval("g_beh_term", "repo_up", 12) > 0, "term deposits rise after a hike")
guard(abs(lpv("c_savings", 4, "lp") - lpv("c_savings", 4, "ardl")) < 0.2, "savings: ARDL matches the local projection")
guard(lpv("g_mortgages_res", 4, "lp") > 0 && lpv("g_mortgages_res", 4, "ardl") < 0, "home loans: the local projection shows the policy reaction")
guard(lpv("c_current", 4, "ardl") < lpv("c_current", 4, "lo"), "current accounts: the ARDL passes through less than the local projection")
dep1 <- vapply(c("c_call", "c_savings", "c_current", "c_ncd"), function(t) mval(t, "repo_up", 1), 0)
guard(dep1[["c_call"]] > 0.6 && dep1[["c_ncd"]] < 0.3 && mval("c_ncd", "repo_up", 4) > 0.75, "deposit repricing speeds")
guard(mval("c_fixed_notice", "repo_up", 12) > 0.8 && mval("c_ncd", "repo_up", 12) > 0.8 &&
        mval("c_current", "repo_up", 12) < min(vapply(c("c_savings", "c_call", "c_fixed_notice", "c_ncd"), function(t) mval(t, "repo_up", 12), 0)),
      "deposit pass-through ordering")
guard(mval("s_vaf", "repo_up", 1) < -0.2 && abs(mval("s_vaf", "repo_up", 12)) < 0.1 && mval("s_cards", "repo_up", 1) < -0.2 &&
        abs(mval("s_cards", "repo_up", 12)) < 0.1, "loan spreads dip and close")
vol3 <- vapply(c("g_personal_other", "g_cards", "g_vaf", "g_mortgages_res"), function(t) mval(t, "repo_up", 12), 0)
guard(all(diff(vol3) > 0) && all(abs(vapply(names(vol3), function(t) mval(t, "repo_up", 4), 0)) < 0.6),
      "unsecured books respond most, and little happens in the first year")
guard(mval("g_cards", "gdp_down", 12) < -1 && mval("g_corp_all", "gdp_down", 12) < -1, "GDP effects on cards and corporate loans")
guard(abs(tdg$phi - 0.995) < 1e-9, "the disaggregation's phi sits at the top of the range searched")
## monthly against quarterly multipliers
mvm <- function(t, q) mval(t, "repo_up", q, st = "monthly")
dep5 <- c("c_call", "c_savings", "c_current", "c_fixed_notice", "c_ncd")
guard(mvm("c_call", 2/3) > 0.5 && mvm("c_ncd", 1/3) < 0.1 && mvm("c_ncd", 2/3) > 0.4 && mvm("c_fixed_notice", 1/3) < 0.1 &&
        mvm("c_fixed_notice", 2/3) > 0.25 && mvm("c_savings", 2/3) < 0.4 && mvm("c_current", 2/3) < 0.4,
      "monthly repricing claims")
guard(max(abs(vapply(dep5, function(t) mvm(t, 12) - mval(t, "repo_up", 12), 0))) < 0.15,
      "long-run deposit pass-through agrees across frequencies")
guard(all(abs(vapply(c("g_cards", "g_vaf", "g_personal_other"), function(t) mvm(t, 12) - mval(t, "repo_up", 12), 0)) < 0.6),
      "unsecured lending agrees across frequencies")
guard(mvm("g_nmd", 4) > 0 && abs(mvm("g_nmd", 12)) < 0.5 && mval("g_nmd", "repo_up", 12) < -1 &&
        mval("g_nmd", "repo_up", 12, col = "lo") < 0 && mval("g_nmd", "repo_up", 12, col = "hi") > 0 &&
        mval("g_nmd", "repo_up", 12, st = "monthly", col = "lo") < 0 && mval("g_nmd", "repo_up", 12, st = "monthly", col = "hi") > 0,
      "non-maturity deposits: the frequencies disagree, both bands span zero")
guard(mvm("g_mortgages_res", 4) > -0.15 && mval("g_mortgages_res", "repo_up", 4) > -0.15 && mvm("g_mortgages_res", 12) < 0 &&
        abs(mvm("g_mortgages_res", 12)) < abs(mval("g_mortgages_res", "repo_up", 12)), "home loans: both frequencies, second year, monthly smaller")
rate_drv <- c("repo", "d_repo", "d4_repo", "real_repo", "repo_pos", "repo_neg", "d_repo_pos", "d_repo_neg")
lagw_avg <- function(t, fq) { z <- DY$lag_profile[DY$lag_profile$target == t & DY$lag_profile$freq == fq & DY$lag_profile$driver %in% rate_drv, ]
  sum(z$lag * z$w) / sum(z$w) }
guard(all(vapply(c("g_mortgages_res", "g_personal_other"), function(t) lagw_avg(t, "month") > 3.9, TRUE)) &&
        lagw_avg("g_mortgages_res", "quarter") < 3.5 && lagw_avg("g_personal_other", "quarter") > 3.5,
      "monthly volume lags sit at the boundary")
guard(all(outer(dep5, c("month", "quarter"), Vectorize(function(t, fq) lagw_avg(t, fq))) < 1.15),
      "deposit costs: rate effect within about a quarter")
guard(abs(lagw_avg("g_mortgages_res", "month") - lagw_avg("g_personal_other", "month")) < 0.05 &&
        abs(mvm("c_savings", 2/3) - mvm("c_current", 2/3)) < 0.03 && MM$sats_m$c_savings$fit$coef[["ar1"]] > 0.9,
      "wording: equal lags, equal two-month moves, monthly savings rho near one")
```

South African banking data are richer at monthly frequency than the
quarterly models use: BA900 is a monthly return for every bank, BA120 (the
sector's income statement) is monthly, and so are the policy rate, bond
yields, inflation, the rand, equity prices, the SARB's coincident indicator
and its credit statistics. Real GDP, the unemployment rate and house prices
are not. This chapter builds the monthly version of Stage 1, tests it against
the quarterly one on the same outcomes, asks whether ARDL is still the right
tool at that frequency, and uses the satellites to show what rates and growth
do to each line of the balance sheet.

```{r m-data-note}

      sprintf("by %s pp on average for savings deposits (at most %s pp), and by up to %s pp for current accounts and NCDs in 2008-09.",
              num(dgv("c_savings", "mean_abs_gap"), 2), num(dgv("c_savings", "max_abs_gap"), 2),
              num(max(dgv("c_current", "max_abs_gap"), dgv("c_ncd", "max_abs_gap")), 1)),

```

## Quarterly series to monthly: the Kalman filter

A monthly model needs monthly GDP, and the monthly path has to satisfy two
conditions: its three months must add up to the published quarter, and its
shape within the quarter should come from monthly data, not from a smooth
curve drawn through the quarters. That is temporal disaggregation (Chow and
Lin, 1971; Fernández, 1981; Litterman, 1983), and its natural home is the
state-space form (Harvey and Pierse, 1984; Proietti, 2006):

$$y_t = x_t'\beta + u_t, \qquad u_t = \phi\, u_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \qquad Y_q = \sum_{t \in q} c\, y_t ,$$

where $y_t$ is the unobserved monthly series, $x_t$ the monthly indicators,
$u_t$ the part the indicators miss, and $Y_q$ the published quarter. A
"cumulator" state adds up the months of each quarter and is observed only in
its last month; the two months in between are missing observations, which
the Kalman filter handles by skipping the update. $\beta$ is estimated by
generalised least squares on the quarters, $\phi$ by maximising the profile
likelihood, and the monthly path is the Kalman smoother's estimate, with a
standard error for every month. The same path has a closed form (the GLS best
linear unbiased predictor); the package computes both and its tests check that
they agree to machine precision. Months after the last published quarter, for
which the indicators already exist, are extrapolated: a nowcast.

Which indicators? The test is out of sample: for each quarter from 2012, the
model is estimated on the quarters before it and the indicators up to its end,
and the three months it extrapolates are summed into a nowcast of the quarter.

```{r m-nowcast}
#| echo: false
ind_lab <- c(none = "None (smooth path)", coinc = "Coincident indicator", `mfg + retail` = "Manufacturing + retail",
             `coinc + mfg + retail` = "Coincident + manufacturing + retail")
mod_lab <- c(`chow-lin` = "Chow-Lin", fernandez = "Fernández", litterman = "Litterman")
guard(all(nc$indicators %in% names(ind_lab)) && all(nc$model %in% names(mod_lab)), "nowcast table labels")
kt(data.frame(Indicators = ind_lab[nc$indicators], Model = mod_lab[nc$model], Quarters = nc$n,
              `RMSE, all` = num(nc$rmse, 2), `RMSE, excluding 2020` = num(nc$rmse_ex2020, 2),
              `AR(1), all` = num(nc$rmse_ar1, 2), `AR(1), excluding 2020` = num(nc$rmse_ar1_ex2020, 2),
              check.names = FALSE), align = "llrrrrr",
   caption = "Out-of-sample nowcasts of quarterly real GDP growth (annualised, percentage points), 2012Q1-2026Q1. Indicators: the SARB coincident business-cycle indicator, manufacturing production and retail sales at constant prices. The AR(1) uses quarterly GDP only.")
```

The coincident indicator with manufacturing and retail sales, in a Chow-Lin
model, nowcasts GDP growth with an error of `r num(best_nc$rmse_ex2020, 2)` pp outside 2020
against `r num(best_nc$rmse_ar1_ex2020, 2)` pp for an AR(1) that sees no monthly data, so its
monthly path carries real information about the quarter; a path with no
indicators (`r num(ncv("none", "litterman", "rmse_ex2020"), 2)` pp) does not. The estimated $\phi$ is
`r num(tdg$phi, 3)`, the top of the range searched: the gap between GDP and the
indicators behaves almost like a random walk (Fernández's case), which is why
the filter re-anchors to every published quarter. Unemployment (published quarterly only since the Quarterly Labour
Force Survey began in 2008) and house prices have no monthly indicator here,
so they get the smooth path whose quarterly averages match (a Litterman model
without regressors).

```{r m-gdp}
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Real GDP growth: the published quarters (annualised quarter on quarter) and the monthly path from the Kalman filter (annualised three-month growth), 2015-2026; the 2020 collapse and rebound run off the scale. The last three months are a nowcast from the indicators."
gm <- MM$disaggregation$gdp_monthly
gm$g3 <- 400 * (log(gm$gdp_m) - log(c(rep(NA, 3), utils::head(gm$gdp_m, -3))))
gq <- P$macro[, c("date", "gdp_qq")]
gq <- gq[gq$date >= as.Date("2015-01-01") & is.finite(gq$gdp_qq), ]
gm <- gm[gm$date >= as.Date("2015-01-01"), ]
ggplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_step(data = transform(gq, date = date - 91), aes(date, gdp_qq, colour = "Published quarter"), linewidth = 0.5,
            direction = "hv") +
  geom_line(data = gm, aes(date, g3, colour = "Monthly path (Kalman)"), linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Published quarter` = ink[["muted"]], `Monthly path (Kalman)` = ent_col[["NGFB"]]), name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-15, 15)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "annualised growth (%)") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Monthly against quarterly

The monthly satellites are built exactly like the quarterly ones -- the same
registry of targets, candidate drivers, economic signs and driver groups,
the same $|t| \ge 1$ and $|\rho| < 0.98$ screens, model averaging with BIC
weights -- with three changes the frequency forces: lags of 0, 1, 2, 3, 6, 9
and 12 months; month-of-year dummies (and the COVID quarters month by month);
and the dynamic out-of-sample selection run twelve months ahead from
quarter-end origins. Monthly interest is annualised with the month's day
count, since interest accrues by the day (a first pass annualised it by
twelve, which reads every February as a fall in rates).

The comparison is the one that matters: both models forecast the *same
quarterly outcomes* from the *same origins*, re-estimated on data up to each
origin and simulated forward along the realised macro path, exactly as in a
scenario. Monthly forecasts map into quarters exactly: three months of
annualised growth average to the quarter's growth, and day-weighted monthly
interest rates sum to the quarterly rate.

```{r m-race}
#| fig-height: 5.8
#| fig-cap: "Forecast error of the monthly ARDL relative to the quarterly ARDL (RMSE ratio; below one, monthly is better), by target and horizon. Same quarterly outcomes, same origins."
rr <- rw
rr$lab <- vapply(rr$target, function(t) S1$sats[[t]]$label %||% t, "")
rr$lab <- factor(rr$lab, levels = unique(rr$lab[order(rr$family, rr$target)]))
rr$block <- ifelse(rr$block == "h1_4", "1-4 quarters ahead", "5-8 quarters ahead")
rr$family <- fam_lab[rr$family]
ggplot(rr, aes(r_m_ardl, lab, colour = family)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ block) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Volumes = ent_col[["Big Four"]], Pricing = ent_col[["NGFB"]],
                                 `Credit losses` = pal$categorical[[7]], `Fees and costs` = ink[["muted"]]),
                      breaks = unname(fam_lab), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "RMSE, monthly / quarterly (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r m-race-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
tw <- merge(rw[rw$block == "h1_4", c("target", "q_ardl", "r_m_ardl")], rw[rw$block == "h5_8", c("target", "r_m_ardl")],
            by = "target", suffixes = c("", "_long"))
tw <- merge(tw, dm, by = "target")
twin(data.frame(Target = vapply(tw$target, function(t) S1$sats[[t]]$label %||% t, ""),
                `Quarterly RMSE, 1-4 q` = num(tw$q_ardl, 3), `Monthly / quarterly, 1-4 q` = num(tw$r_m_ardl, 2),
                `Monthly / quarterly, 5-8 q` = num(tw$r_m_ardl_long, 2),
                `Diebold-Mariano (positive favours monthly)` = num(tw$dm_stat, 2), `p-value` = num(tw$p_value, 3),
                check.names = FALSE), "Table view: monthly against quarterly, with Diebold-Mariano tests (1-4 quarters)")
```

**Monthly estimation does not fit better, with one informative exception.**
For pricing, the family where monthly data were expected to help most, the
median monthly model's error is `r num(med("pricing", "m_ardl", "h1_4"), 2)` times the quarterly model's one to four
quarters ahead and `r num(med("pricing", "m_ardl", "h5_8"), 2)` times five to eight quarters ahead, and
`r num(med_own("pricing", "h1_4"), 2)` times when the monthly models are scored on their own definition
of the quarterly rate; for volumes the ratios are `r num(med("volume", "m_ardl", "h1_4"), 2)` and
`r num(med("volume", "m_ardl", "h5_8"), 2)`. Of the `r nrow(dm)` Diebold-Mariano tests, `r n_q_better` reject
equal accuracy in favour of the quarterly model at 10% and `r n_m_better` in favour of the
monthly: corporate loans (error ratio `r num(rwt("g_corp_all", "r_m_ardl"), 2)`) and term deposits
(`r num(rwt("g_beh_term", "r_m_ardl"), 2)`), both at the 1% level. The credit-loss ratio
(`r num(med("credit", "m_ardl", "h1_4"), 2)` near term) and operating costs are also forecast better monthly,
but not significantly.

The exception is the lumpiest business in the sector: corporate drawdowns and
repayments, and institutional term placements, which partly reverse the next
month (month-on-month growth has a first-order autocorrelation of
`r num(lag1_m[["g_corp_all"]], 2)` for corporate loans and `r num(lag1_m[["g_beh_term"]], 2)` for term
deposits). A quarterly model sees only that the quarter grew; a monthly model
sees *when* in the quarter the lump arrived, and so whether its reversal is
still to come. The gain is in the dynamics, not in the macro response: a
monthly AR(1) with no macro drivers does as well (`r num(rwt("g_corp_all", "r_m_ar1"), 2)` and
`r num(rwt("g_beh_term", "r_m_ar1"), 2)`). Across all volumes, the monthly AR(1) is the most accurate
short-horizon forecaster of the eight (median ratio `r num(med("volume", "m_ar1", "h1_4"), 2)`, against
`r num(med("volume", "q_ar1", "h1_4"), 2)` for the quarterly AR(1)): the latest month carries momentum
that a quarterly series reports late.

Why monthly data do not help more generally is a matter of signal and noise.
The signal in these series is slow: a deposit book reprices over quarters, a credit cycle turns over years,
and the policy rate moves only at the six MPC meetings a year, so monthly
timing adds a few weeks of resolution at most. The noise is per observation:
month-end balances, interest posted unevenly across months, provisions booked
at quarter and year ends. Tripling the observations triples the noise draws
without adding much independent information about slow dynamics, and in the
monthly pricing models the autoregressive coefficient sits close to one
(`r num(MM$sats_m$c_savings$fit$coef[["ar1"]], 2)` for savings deposits), where small estimation errors
compound over a 24-month simulation. Quarterly aggregation is not a
loss of information here; it is a filter.

**So the production models stay quarterly.** Monthly data still earn their
place in two ways the evidence supports: the Kalman filter's monthly GDP
path is a genuine nowcast of the quarter in progress, and the latest month of
BA900 and BA120 can update the jump-off book before the quarter closes --
above all for corporate loans and term deposits, where a monthly view of the
jump-off is significantly more accurate. Neither argues for monthly scenario
models. What a three-year scenario needs from Stage 1 is the macro response,
and on that the two frequencies broadly agree where it matters most for
earnings, deposit pricing and unsecured lending (see the multipliers below).

## Is ARDL still the right tool at monthly frequency?

The same race includes the two alternatives that make most sense when the lag
dimension grows from five quarters to thirteen months: **polynomial
distributed lags** (Almon), in which each driver enters through a quadratic
lag profile over 0-12 months, so a rate change can be spread over a year with
three parameters instead of thirteen, the sign restriction applying to the
sum of the lag weights; and **Bayesian shrinkage**, the single-equation
version of a Bayesian VAR with exogenous drivers, in which every candidate
driver enters at every lag, coefficients are shrunk towards zero with a prior
variance that falls with the lag (a Minnesota prior), and the tightness is set
by the marginal likelihood -- shrinkage instead of selection, and no signs.

```{r m-classes}
#| echo: false
ct <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("h1_4", "h5_8"), function(b) do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fam_lab), function(f)
  data.frame(`Quarters ahead` = ifelse(b == "h1_4", "1-4", "5-8"), Family = fam_lab[[f]],
             `ARDL, quarterly` = "1.00", `PDL, quarterly` = num(med(f, "q_pdl", b), 2),
             `Shrinkage, quarterly` = num(med(f, "q_shrink", b), 2), `AR(1), quarterly` = num(med(f, "q_ar1", b), 2),
             `ARDL, monthly` = num(med(f, "m_ardl", b), 2), `PDL, monthly` = num(med(f, "m_pdl", b), 2),
             `Shrinkage, monthly` = num(med(f, "m_shrink", b), 2), `AR(1), monthly` = num(med(f, "m_ar1", b), 2),
             check.names = FALSE)))))
kt(ct, align = "llrrrrrrrr",
   caption = paste0("Median forecast error by model class, relative to the quarterly sign-restricted ARDL average (below one is better). Same quarterly outcomes and origins for every model. PDL: polynomial distributed lags.",
                    if (length(no_pdl_q)) sprintf(" No quarterly PDL specification for %s survives the sign and t screens, so that median covers the other volume targets.",
                                                  tolower(paste(plab[sub("^g_", "", no_pdl_q)], collapse = " and "))) else ""))
```

**Yes.** Within each frequency the sign-restricted ARDL average is the most
accurate macro model for pricing, ahead of both alternatives: polynomial lags
impose a smooth lag profile that deposit repricing does not have (it is a
jump at the MPC meeting followed by a tail), and shrinkage keeps every
driver at every lag with small, often wrong-signed coefficients that add noise.
For volumes no macro model beats a plain AR(1) one to eight quarters ahead
(median ratio `r num(med("volume", "q_ar1", "h1_4"), 2)`, and `r num(med("volume", "m_ar1", "h1_4"), 2)` for the monthly AR(1)): a loan
book's next quarter is mostly its last quarter. The macro information in volumes is in where a three-year
scenario path ends, not in next quarter's growth, which is why the satellites
are chosen on multi-step accuracy and held to economic signs rather than
fitted for the shortest horizon.

A VAR would not change this. In a scenario the macro path is set from
outside, so the object needed is the distribution of each banking variable
*conditional on* that path. A VAR's conditional forecast (Waggoner and Zha,
1999) equals the ARDL's when the macro block does not respond to the banking
variables within the horizon; otherwise the VAR adds equations for macro
variables that the scenario then overrides. The VAR's real advantage, joint
dynamics, matters for unconditional forecasting, not for scenario analysis.

Mixed-frequency regressions (MIDAS; Ghysels, Santa-Clara and Valkanov, 2004)
solve a different problem: a target observed only quarterly, with drivers
observed monthly. Here the targets are monthly too, so the monthly ARDL uses
strictly more information than a MIDAS regression of the quarterly target on
monthly drivers would, and the polynomial lags above are MIDAS's weighting
scheme applied at a single frequency.

## How the lags are chosen and how the sign restrictions work

Each satellite is a model average over a disciplined search, not a single
regression. For a target $y$ with candidate drivers $x_j$:

1. **Specifications.** Every subset of at most `r CFG$max_k` drivers, at most one
   from each economic group (the repo level and its change never compete in
   one equation, unless the target's registry allows both), each at **one**
   lag chosen from a grid -- 0 to 4 quarters (0 to 12 months monthly):
   $y_t = c + \rho\, y_{t-1} + \sum_j \beta_j x_{j,t-\ell_j} + \varepsilon_t$.
   One lag per driver keeps the parameter count down; the AR term $\rho$
   spreads the effect over time, so the response to a permanent change in
   $x_j$ is $0$ before $\ell_j$ and then
   $\beta_j(1 + \rho + \dots + \rho^{h-\ell_j})$, converging to the long-run
   multiplier $\beta_j / (1 - \rho)$.
2. **Sign restrictions.** A specification survives only if every driver's
   short-run coefficient $\beta_j$ *and* long-run multiplier
   $\beta_j/(1-\rho)$ carry the sign economics requires (a higher repo rate
   cannot raise mortgage demand; higher unemployment cannot lower credit
   losses), where the registry fixes one, with $|t_{\text{HAC}}| \ge 1$, and
   $|\rho| < 0.98$. This is a restriction on the *model space*, not on a
   structural shock as in a sign-restricted VAR: it removes specifications
   whose estimated effects contradict the direction economics requires.
   Where theory is ambiguous the sign is left free: the policy rate for
   cards and corporate credit (a hike damps new borrowing but raises
   drawdowns on existing facilities as cash flow tightens) and for
   non-maturity deposits (higher rates draw money into savings and notice
   accounts and push it out to term deposits).
3. **Selection.** Survivors are ranked by dynamic pseudo-out-of-sample error
   -- re-estimated at each origin and simulated four quarters ahead along the
   realised macro path -- and the most parsimonious within 2% of the best is
   the selected specification.
4. **Averaging.** Projections average every surviving specification with BIC
   weights, an approximation to posterior model probabilities (Raftery,
   1995), so lag uncertainty is carried into the scenario rather than
   resolved by fiat.

Home loans show how this works. Of the
`r format(sgv("g_mortgages_res", "n_specs"), big.mark = ",")` candidate specifications,
`r sgv("g_mortgages_res", "sign_valid")` survive the screens. The model average puts
`r pct(sum(hl_d4), 0)` of its weight on the four-quarter change in the repo rate, spread
over lags of two quarters (`r pct(hl_d4[["2"]], 0)`), three (`r pct(hl_d4[["3"]], 0)`) and four
(`r pct(hl_d4[["4"]], 0)`); the one-quarter change and the repo level carry the rest of
the rate weight, also at two to four quarters, and specifications with house
prices carry `r pct(hpi_w("g_mortgages_res"), 0)`. No single lag is imposed: a rate rise starts
to slow home-loan growth after about two quarters and keeps slowing it for
well over a year (at most `r pct(hl_rate_early, 0)` of the weight sits on lags of zero or
one quarter). The selected specification, the four-quarter
change at a two-quarter lag, is the most parsimonious within 2% of the best
out-of-sample error; the scenarios use the average.

```{r m-signs}
#| echo: false
sg <- stats::aggregate(cbind(n_specs, rejected_sign, rejected_t, rejected_rho, sign_valid) ~ family, sgc, sum)
wf <- stats::aggregate(cbind(wrong_weight_free, ratio = rmse_free / rmse_restricted) ~ family, sgc, stats::median)
sg <- merge(sg, wf, by = "family")
kt(data.frame(Family = fam_lab[sg$family], Specifications = format(sg$n_specs, big.mark = ","),
              `Fail a sign` = pct(sg$rejected_sign / sg$n_specs, 0), `Fail the t screen` = pct(sg$rejected_t / sg$n_specs, 0),
              `Fail the ρ screen` = pct(sg$rejected_rho / sg$n_specs, 0), `Survive` = format(sg$sign_valid, big.mark = ","),
              `Wrong-sign weight, unrestricted` = pct(sg$wrong_weight_free, 0),
              `RMSE, unrestricted / restricted` = num(sg$ratio, 2), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lrrrrrrr",
   caption = "What the restrictions remove, quarterly production models. The last two columns re-run the search with every sign left free: the share of the model-average weight that lands on specifications with at least one economically wrong sign, and the out-of-sample error of that average relative to the restricted one (1-4 quarters); both are medians across the family's targets.")
```

The restrictions matter exactly where the data are misleading. For pricing,
the data and economics agree: without the restriction almost no weight lands
on a wrong sign and accuracy is unchanged. For volumes they disagree. In home
loans `r pct(sgv("g_mortgages_res", "rejected_sign") / sgv("g_mortgages_res", "n_specs"), 0)` of
the `r format(sgv("g_mortgages_res", "n_specs"), big.mark = ",")` specifications fail a sign, and with the signs left free
`r pct(sgv("g_mortgages_res", "wrong_weight_free"), 0)` of the model weight goes to specifications in which a higher
repo rate *raises* mortgage growth. That is not a finding about mortgages;
it is the SARB at work: it hikes into credit booms and cuts into slumps, so in
the raw data rates and credit growth rise together. The unrestricted average
learns that correlation and forecasts worse out of sample
(`r num(sgv("g_mortgages_res", "rmse_free"), 2)` against `r num(sgv("g_mortgages_res", "rmse_restricted"), 2)`), and in a scenario it
would turn a hike into a lending boom. The credit-loss ratio is the
instructive exception: the free model forecasts slightly better near term
(`r num(sgv("clr", "rmse_free"), 3)` against `r num(sgv("clr", "rmse_restricted"), 3)`), with all of its weight on wrong signs;
the restricted model gives up a little short-horizon fit for the right causal
direction, which is what a stress scenario needs.

```{r m-lags}
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-cap: "Where the rate effect sits: the model-averaged lag (in quarters) of the policy-rate drivers in each satellite, quarterly production models and monthly models (monthly volumes are shown only when they come from BA900). Larger points: more of the model weight on that driver."
lp_rate <- DY$lag_profile[DY$lag_profile$driver %in% c("repo", "d_repo", "d4_repo", "real_repo", "repo_pos",
                                                         "repo_neg", "d_repo_pos", "d_repo_neg"), ]
if (MM$vol_source == "KBP") lp_rate <- lp_rate[!(lp_rate$freq == "month" & grepl("^g_", lp_rate$target)), ]
lp_rate$lab <- vapply(lp_rate$target, function(t) S1$sats[[t]]$label %||% t, "")
lp_rate$freq <- ifelse(lp_rate$freq == "quarter", "Quarterly", "Monthly")
ggplot(lp_rate, aes(lag, lab, colour = freq)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = w), alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1, 4), guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Quarterly = ent_col[["Big Four"]], Monthly = ent_col[["NGFB"]]), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "model-averaged lag of the rate driver (quarters)", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Deposit costs carry their rate effect within about a quarter at both
frequencies. Retail loan books are the opposite: the monthly models put
almost all of their rate weight at the longest lag the grid allows, twelve
months, for home loans and personal loans (both at `r num(lagw_avg("g_mortgages_res", "month"), 1)` quarters), and
the quarterly models, whose grid
reaches the same year, at `r num(lagw_avg("g_mortgages_res", "quarter"), 1)` and
`r num(lagw_avg("g_personal_other", "quarter"), 1)` quarters. Both frequencies say a rate change takes
the best part of a year to reach a retail loan book; at the boundary, the
monthly grid cannot say whether it takes longer.

## Dynamic multipliers: what a rate move does to each line

A dynamic multiplier is the path of a line after a shock, all else equal.
Because the satellites average several specifications whose rate drivers
include the level, its one- and four-period changes, the real rate and the
partial sums of hikes and cuts, the multipliers are computed by simulation:
each model is projected along a flat macro path and along the same path with
the shock, every derived driver recomputed (a repo shock moves prime, JIBAR,
the real rate, the changes and the partial sums together), and the difference
is the multiplier. Bands redraw the coefficients of the averaged
specifications from their HAC covariance (5th to 95th percentile).

```{r m-mult-vol}
#| fig-height: 5.2
#| fig-cap: "A permanent 100 bps rise in the repo rate: the level of sector balances, percent difference from no change, quarterly production models with a 90% parameter band (all else equal: the macro path is otherwise unchanged)."
vt <- c("g_mortgages_res", "g_mortgages_com", "g_vaf", "g_cards", "g_personal_other", "g_corp_all", "g_nmd", "g_beh_term")
mv1 <- mu[mu$set == "production" & mu$shock == "repo_up" & mu$target %in% vt, ]
mv1$lab <- factor(plab[sub("^g_", "", mv1$target)], levels = plab)
ggplot(mv1, aes(quarters, effect)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = ent_col[["NGFB"]], alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(colour = ent_col[["NGFB"]], linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ lab, ncol = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 4, 8, 12)) +
  labs(x = "quarters after the rise", y = "balance, % difference")
```

```{r m-mult-vol-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
tv <- do.call(rbind, lapply(vt, function(t) data.frame(Line = plab[sub("^g_", "", t)],
  `After 1 year` = sprintf("%+.2f", mval(t, "repo_up", 4)), `After 2 years` = sprintf("%+.2f", mval(t, "repo_up", 8)),
  `After 3 years` = sprintf("%+.2f", mval(t, "repo_up", 12)),
  `90% band, 3 years` = sprintf("%+.2f to %+.2f", mval(t, "repo_up", 12, col = "lo"), mval(t, "repo_up", 12, col = "hi")),
  check.names = FALSE)))
twin(tv, "Table view: balances after a permanent 100 bps rise in the repo rate (% difference)")
```

Loan books respond slowly and unsecured lending most: three years after a
permanent 100 bps rise, personal loans are
`r sprintf("%.1f", abs(mval("g_personal_other", "repo_up", 12)))`% smaller than they would have been, cards
`r sprintf("%.1f", abs(mval("g_cards", "repo_up", 12)))`%, vehicle and asset finance `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(mval("g_vaf", "repo_up", 12)))`% and home loans
`r sprintf("%.1f", abs(mval("g_mortgages_res", "repo_up", 12)))`%, with little happening in the first year. Term deposits
*grow* (`r sprintf("%+.1f", mval("g_beh_term", "repo_up", 12))`%): savers move into fixed deposits when rates are high. These are partial
effects with the rest of the macro path held fixed; in a scenario a hike also
slows GDP and raises unemployment, which add their own effects through the
other drivers.

```{r m-mult-price}
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "A permanent 100 bps change in the repo rate: deposit costs and loan spreads over their reference rates (percentage points), quarterly production models. Solid: a rise; dashed: a cut (shown with its sign reversed, so that a symmetric response would overlap)."
pt <- c("c_current", "c_savings", "c_call", "c_fixed_notice", "c_ncd", "s_homeloans", "s_vaf", "s_cards")
mp <- mu[mu$set == "production" & mu$target %in% pt & mu$shock %in% c("repo_up", "repo_down"), ]
mp$effect[mp$shock == "repo_down"] <- -mp$effect[mp$shock == "repo_down"]
mp$lab <- factor(tlab[mp$target], levels = tlab[pt])
mp$shock <- ifelse(mp$shock == "repo_up", "Rise", "Cut (sign reversed)")
ggplot(mp, aes(quarters, effect, linetype = shock)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(colour = ent_col[["NGFB"]], linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ lab, ncol = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 4, 8, 12)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Rise = "solid", `Cut (sign reversed)` = "22"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "quarters after the change", y = "percentage points") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Deposit costs reprice at very different speeds. Call deposits move almost at
once (`r num(mval("c_call", "repo_up", 1), 2)` pp in the first quarter after a 100 bps rise); savings and
current accounts move part of the way (`r num(mval("c_savings", "repo_up", 1), 2)` and
`r num(mval("c_current", "repo_up", 1), 2)`); NCDs only as they roll over (`r num(mval("c_ncd", "repo_up", 1), 2)` at first,
`r num(mval("c_ncd", "repo_up", 4), 2)` after a year). After three years fixed and notice deposits and NCDs
have passed through almost fully (`r num(mval("c_fixed_notice", "repo_up", 12), 2)` and `r num(mval("c_ncd", "repo_up", 12), 2)`)
and current accounts least (`r num(mval("c_current", "repo_up", 12), 2)`). Savings deposits show the asymmetry:
a 100 bps rise adds `r num(mval("c_savings", "repo_up", 12), 2)` pp to their cost after three years, a 100 bps
cut takes off only `r num(abs(mval("c_savings", "repo_down", 12)), 2)` pp, which is what squeezes the savings
margin in an easing cycle. Loan yields are set off prime, which moves one for one
with the repo rate, so their spreads dip on impact (the book reprices with a
lag) and close within a year or two: vehicle and asset finance by
`r num(abs(mval("s_vaf", "repo_up", 1)), 2)` pp at first and cards by `r num(abs(mval("s_cards", "repo_up", 1)), 2)` pp.

### The first months, seen monthly

The quarterly models report the first quarter as one number. The monthly
models, estimated on the same lines with the same signs, show what happens
inside it.

```{r m-mult-freq}
#| fig-height: 5.2
#| fig-cap: "A permanent 100 bps rise in the repo rate, monthly models (line, month by month) against the quarterly production models (points, one per quarter): deposit costs in percentage points, balances in % difference. The first three years."
ft <- c("c_call", "c_savings", "c_current", "c_fixed_notice", "c_ncd", "g_cards", "g_mortgages_res", "g_nmd")
mf <- mu[mu$shock == "repo_up" & mu$target %in% ft & mu$set %in% c("production", "monthly"), ]
mf$lab <- factor(tlab[mf$target], levels = tlab[ft])
mf$set <- ifelse(mf$set == "production", "Quarterly", "Monthly")
ggplot(mf, aes(quarters, effect, colour = set)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = mf[mf$set == "Monthly", ], linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(data = mf[mf$set == "Quarterly", ], size = 1.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ lab, ncol = 4, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 4, 8, 12)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Monthly = ent_col[["NGFB"]], Quarterly = ent_col[["Big Four"]]), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "quarters after the rise", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r m-mult-freq-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
tf <- do.call(rbind, lapply(ft, function(t) data.frame(Line = tlab[[t]],
  `Month 1` = sprintf("%+.2f", mvm(t, 1/3)), `Month 2` = sprintf("%+.2f", mvm(t, 2/3)),
  `Quarter 1, monthly` = sprintf("%+.2f", mvm(t, 1)), `Quarter 1, quarterly` = sprintf("%+.2f", mval(t, "repo_up", 1)),
  `Year 3, monthly` = sprintf("%+.2f", mvm(t, 12)), `Year 3, quarterly` = sprintf("%+.2f", mval(t, "repo_up", 12)),
  check.names = FALSE)))
twin(tf, "Table view: monthly against quarterly multipliers (deposit costs in pp, balances in %)")
```

Call deposits have repriced `r ubps(mvm("c_call", 2/3) / 100)` two months after a 100 bps
rise. NCDs barely move in the first month (`r bps(mvm("c_ncd", 1/3) / 100)`) and then
reprice `r ubps(mvm("c_ncd", 2/3) / 100)` in the second as certificates roll over; fixed and
notice deposits follow the same pattern. Savings and current accounts have
each moved about `r ubps(mean(c(mvm("c_savings", 2/3), mvm("c_current", 2/3))) / 100)` after two months. After three years the monthly and quarterly models are within
`r num(max(abs(vapply(dep5, function(t) mvm(t, 12) - mval(t, "repo_up", 12), 0))), 2)` pp of each other on every
deposit line, so for NII over a scenario the frequency hardly matters; for the
first quarter of a rate cycle -- the quarter an ALCO is usually asked about --
the monthly profile is the better guide. For balances the two frequencies
agree on unsecured lending (cards `r sprintf("%+.1f", mvm("g_cards", 12))`% monthly against
`r sprintf("%+.1f", mval("g_cards", "repo_up", 12))`% quarterly after three years) and on the timing of home
loans, which slow only from the second year (the monthly response is smaller,
`r sprintf("%+.1f", mvm("g_mortgages_res", 12))`% against `r sprintf("%+.1f", mval("g_mortgages_res", "repo_up", 12))`%). They disagree on
non-maturity deposits, where the monthly model finds a small, temporary inflow (`r sprintf("%+.1f", mvm("g_nmd", 4))`% after a year) and the
quarterly model a gradual outflow (`r sprintf("%+.1f", mval("g_nmd", "repo_up", 12))`% after three years),
both with bands that span zero: volume elasticities remain the least well
identified part of Stage 1.

```{r m-mult-gdp}
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-cap: "GDP growth one percentage point lower, permanently: the sector's credit-loss ratio (percentage points) and loan balances (% difference), quarterly production models."
gt <- c("clr", "g_mortgages_res", "g_vaf", "g_cards", "g_personal_other", "g_corp_all")
mg2 <- mu[mu$set == "production" & mu$shock == "gdp_down" & mu$target %in% gt, ]
mg2$lab <- ifelse(mg2$target == "clr", "Credit-loss ratio (pp)", paste0(plab[sub("^g_", "", mg2$target)], " (%)"))
ggplot(mg2, aes(quarters, effect)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = sc_col[["downside"]], alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(colour = sc_col[["downside"]], linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ lab, ncol = 3, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 4, 8, 12)) +
  labs(x = "quarters after the shock", y = NULL)
```

Growth works through credit quality and volumes rather than pricing: a
percentage point less GDP growth raises the sector's credit-loss ratio by
`r num(mval("clr", "gdp_down", 12), 2)` pp after three years (NGFB's unsecured-heavy book multiplies that) and
takes `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(mval("g_cards", "gdp_down", 12)))`% off card balances and
`r sprintf("%.1f", abs(mval("g_corp_all", "gdp_down", 12)))`% off corporate loans.

### A model-free check: local projections

Local projections (Jordà, 2005) estimate the response to a repo change
horizon by horizon, without the ARDL's geometric decay. The comparison feeds
the ARDL the same repo path the projections find (a rate change is followed
by further changes in the same direction).

```{r m-lp}
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| fig-cap: "Response to a 1 pp repo change: local projection (points, 90% band) and the ARDL along the same repo path (line), quarterly. Deposit costs in percentage points; balances in % (the level of the book)."
lpq <- DY$lp[DY$lp$freq == "quarter", ]
lpq$lab <- factor(tlab[lpq$target], levels = unique(tlab[lpq$target]))
ggplot(lpq, aes(h)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), colour = ink[["muted"]], width = 0, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(aes(y = lp), colour = ink[["muted"]], size = 1.4) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ardl), colour = ent_col[["NGFB"]], linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ lab, ncol = 4, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 4, 8, 12)) +
  labs(x = "quarters after the change", y = NULL)
```

For savings and fixed deposits the two agree closely: the savings-deposit
model's response four quarters on is `r num(lpv("c_savings", 4, "ardl"), 2)` pp against the local
projection's `r num(lpv("c_savings", 4, "lp"), 2)`. Current accounts are the exception: along the same
repo path the local projection finds `r num(lpv("c_current", 4, "lp"), 2)` pp after four quarters and the
model `r num(lpv("c_current", 4, "ardl"), 2)`, below the projection's band. If the projection is right,
current-account costs follow the policy rate more closely than the model
assumes, which would make NGFB somewhat more liability-sensitive than
reported. For loan volumes they disagree, and instructively. The
local projection says home-loan balances are *higher* after a rise
(`r sprintf("%+.1f", lpv("g_mortgages_res", 4, "lp"))`% four quarters on): it measures the correlation between rate
changes and credit growth, and the SARB raises rates when credit is strong. It
is model-free but not identification-free; the sign restriction is what
identifies the causal direction in the satellites. A clean test would need
monetary-policy shocks measured directly, for example from the movement of
interest-rate futures around MPC announcements.

# Stage 2: banks relative to the industry

## Regimes and the share model

```{r regimes}
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-cap: "The repo rate with the macro regimes used in Stage 2. Contraction takes priority (real GDP down on a year earlier), then hiking or easing (the repo rate up or down at least 25 bps over two quarters)."
rgm <- S2$regimes
reg_col <- c(contraction = "#e34948", hiking = "#eb6834", easing = "#1baf7a", neutral = "#c3c2b7")
mm <- merge(rgm, P$macro[, c("date", "repo")], by = "date")
mm$start <- mm$date - 91
ggplot(mm) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = start, xmax = date, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = regime), alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(date, repo), colour = ink[["primary"]], linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = reg_col) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "repo rate (%)")
```

For each peer group (and, internally, each large bank) and product, the
annualised change in log market share is

$$ 400\,\Delta \log s_{t} = a + \delta_{\text{contr}}\, C_t + \delta_{\text{hike}}\, H_t + \delta_{\text{ease}}\, E_t + \kappa\,(g^{\text{sector}}_t - \bar g) + e_t , $$

where $a$ is the structural share drift, the $\delta$s are the extra drift in
each regime (neutral is the base), and $\kappa$ is the share's sensitivity to
the sector cycle: $\kappa > 0$ means the bank grows faster than the market in
booms and shrinks faster in busts. The sample has `r sum(rgm$regime == "contraction")`
contraction, `r sum(rgm$regime == "hiking")` hiking, `r sum(rgm$regime == "easing")` easing and
`r sum(rgm$regime == "neutral")` neutral quarters from `r qlab(min(rgm$date))`.

```{r s2-groups}
#| echo: false
keep_p <- c("cards", "personal_other", "mortgages_res", "corp_all", "nmd", "dep_retail", "beh_term")
prod_lab <- c(show_p, dep_retail = "Retail deposits (households)", vaf = "Vehicle and asset finance",
              mortgages_com = "Commercial mortgages")
cg <- S2$coef_groups[S2$coef_groups$product %in% keep_p, ]
cg$cell <- ifelse(is.finite(cg$t), sprintf("%+.1f (%.1f)", cg$est, cg$t), sprintf("%+.1f", cg$est))
dr <- cg[cg$param == "(Intercept)", c("product", "entity", "cell")]
dwd <- stats::reshape(dr, idvar = "product", timevar = "entity", direction = "wide")
names(dwd) <- sub("^cell\\.", "", names(dwd))
for (g in c("Big Four", "Challengers", "Specialists", "Other")) if (!g %in% names(dwd)) dwd[[g]] <- NA
dwd[is.na(dwd)] <- "—"
dwd$product <- prod_lab[dwd$product]
dwd <- dwd[match(prod_lab[keep_p], dwd$product), ]
kt(dwd[, c("product", "Big Four", "Challengers", "Specialists", "Other")], align = "lrrrr",
   caption = "Structural share drift a by peer group: percent a year of share growth, HAC t-statistics in brackets (— where a group's share is too small to model).")
```

```{r s2-groups-full}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cwd <- stats::reshape(cg[, c("entity", "product", "param", "cell")], idvar = c("entity", "product"),
                      timevar = "param", direction = "wide")
names(cwd) <- sub("^cell\\.", "", names(cwd))
cwd <- cwd[, c("product", "entity", "(Intercept)", "contraction", "hiking", "easing", "kappa")]
names(cwd) <- c("Product", "Group", "Drift a", "Contraction", "Hiking", "Easing", "Cycle kappa")
cwd$Product <- prod_lab[cwd$Product]
twin(cwd[order(cwd$Product, cwd$Group), ], "All share-model coefficients (percent a year; HAC t in brackets; kappa per point of sector growth)")
```

The structural drifts carry the clearest message: over 2008–2026 the
Challengers took share at double-digit rates in cards, retail deposits and
non-maturity deposits (all with $t > 2.5$), and the Big Four ceded it slowly
but significantly in cards, retail deposits and mortgages. Regime effects are
mostly imprecise, as is to be expected with only `r sum(rgm$regime == "contraction")`
contraction quarters, which is why they are pooled across banks and then
truncated before they reach NGFB.

## Who takes share from whom

```{r who-gains}
#| fig-height: 5.2
#| fig-cap: "Average change in market share by regime, percentage points a year, with NGFB in the mix. Positive (blue) is a gain."
rs <- N$regime_share
rs <- rs[rs$product %in% c(names(show_p), "dep_retail"), ]
rs$product <- factor(prod_lab[rs$product], levels = rev(prod_lab[c(names(show_p), "dep_retail")]))
rs$entity <- factor(rs$entity, levels = names(ent_col))
rs$regime <- factor(rs$regime, levels = c("contraction", "hiking", "easing", "neutral"))
lim <- max(abs(rs$ds_pp_yr), na.rm = TRUE)
ggplot(rs, aes(entity, product, fill = ds_pp_yr)) +
  geom_tile(colour = ink[["surface"]], linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ regime, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = div_lo, mid = div_mid, high = div_hi, midpoint = 0, limits = c(-lim, lim),
                       name = "pp a year") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1), legend.title = element_text(colour = ink[["secondary"]]),
        panel.grid.major = element_blank())
```

```{r who-gains-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
rw <- stats::reshape(data.frame(product = as.character(rs$product), entity = as.character(rs$entity),
                                regime = as.character(rs$regime), v = sprintf("%+.2f", rs$ds_pp_yr)),
                     idvar = c("product", "entity"), timevar = "regime", direction = "wide")
names(rw) <- sub("^v\\.", "", names(rw))
twin(rw[order(rw$product, rw$entity), ], "Table view (pp a year)")
```

Net share changes do not say who lost to whom: a two-point gain could come
from one competitor or from all of them. The flow matrices below use a
labelled convention, giving each gainer's gain to the losers in proportion to
their losses.

```{r flows}
#| echo: false
fm <- function(key) {
  M <- N$flows[[key]]
  d <- data.frame(`gains` = rownames(M), round(M, 2), check.names = FALSE)
  d[rowSums(abs(M)) > 0, , drop = FALSE]
}
f1 <- fm("cards contraction"); f2 <- fm("nmd hiking")
guard(abs(sum(N$flows[["cards contraction"]]) -
          sum(pmax(rs$ds_pp_yr[rs$regime == "contraction" & rs$product == "Credit cards"], 0))) < 1e-8,
      "flow matrix does not allocate the gains")
kt(f1, caption = "Credit cards in contractions: share gained (rows) from each loser (columns), pp a year.")
kt(f2, caption = "Non-maturity deposits in hiking regimes: share gained (rows) from each loser (columns), pp a year.")
```

In contractions the Big Four lose card share to the Challengers and to
NGFB; in hiking regimes non-maturity deposits move from the Big Four towards
the Specialists, with NGFB and the Challengers smaller gainers. NGFB's rows follow from its drawn
parameters below, so they describe the kind of bank NGFB is, not data about
any real bank.

## NGFB's share parameters

```{r ngfb-draw}
#| echo: false
ph <- S2$population_hyper
ph <- ph[ph$product %in% c("cards", "personal_other", "nmd"), ]
ph$product <- prod_lab[ph$product]
kt(data.frame(Product = ph$product, Parameter = ph$param, `Population mean` = num(ph$mu, 2),
              `Between-bank s.d.` = num(ph$tau, 2), `s.e. of mean` = num(ph$se_mu, 2),
              Banks = ph$k, NGFB = num(ph$ngfb, 2), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "llrrrrr", caption = sprintf("Random-effects (DerSimonian–Laird) pooling across the six large banks and NGFB's posterior-predictive draw (seed %d), truncated at the same central probability mass as Post 1. Only pooled hyperparameters are shown.", CFG$seed))
```

Each parameter is pooled across the six large banks with a random-effects
(DerSimonian–Laird) estimator, and NGFB's vector is drawn from the posterior
predictive $N(\mu, \tau^2 + \text{se}_\mu^2)$, truncated to the same central
probability mass as Post 1 (radius `r num(unique(S2$population_hyper$radius), 2)` in five
dimensions). Only pooled quantities with at least four banks are used. NGFB's
**structural drift is switched off** in all projections: a drawn drift of a
few percent a year compounds into large, arbitrary share gains or losses
over a horizon, and the question here is how NGFB responds to the *cycle*.

# Scenarios {#scenarios}

```{r scen-table}
#| echo: false
lib <- c(SC$library, list(downside_cuts = SC$variants$downside_cuts$scenario))
guard(sum(lib$downside$gdp_yy < 0) >= 8 && max(lib$downside$cpi_yy) > 6 && max(lib$upside$gdp_yy) > 2.9,
      "scenario narratives")
guard(att_r("downside_cuts") / att_r("downside") > 0.35 && att_r("downside_cuts") / att_r("downside") < 0.65,
      "the variant loses about half")
kt(data.frame(Scenario = sc_long[names(lib)], Narrative = vapply(lib, function(s) attr(s, "narrative") %||% "", ""),
              Probability = c(pct(CFG$scenario_weights[scen], 0), "variant"), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "llr", caption = "The three scenarios, and the downside's policy-rate variant. Probabilities are judgemental and are used only for the probability-weighted positioning.")
```

The baseline starts from the realised data at `r qlab(date0)` and follows the
SARB's own guidance for the next year: the repo rate at 7.25% after the
September 2026 increase, inflation above 5% around the turn of the year and
back at the 3% target (adopted with a one-point tolerance band in November
2025) by late 2027, after which the policy rate eases gradually to a
`r num(CFG$anchors$repo, 2)`% neutral level. Growth converges to about
`r num(CFG$anchors$gdp_yy, 1)`%. The upside and the downside are shocks layered on
the baseline with build-up, hold and decay profiles; the derived variables
(prime, JIBAR, curve slope, real rates, rate changes and their partial sums)
are recomputed from the shocked paths, so every scenario is internally
consistent.

The **downside** is deliberately stagflationary. The SARB's own 2023 common
scenario stress test built its domestic adverse scenario the same way: a
higher country risk premium and a sharply weaker rand push inflation up, the
SARB tightens, government bond yields reprice and the economy contracts. The
alternative, a demand-led recession in which inflation falls and the SARB
cuts (2009, 2020), is run as a **variant** with the same real shock, because
for a hedged bank the policy response decides the sign of the rate effect.

```{r macro-paths}
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| fig-cap: "Macro paths by scenario (history in grey). The dashed line is the downside's variant with rate cuts."
mv_lab <- c(repo = "Repo rate (%)", gov10y = "10-year government yield (%)", cpi_yy = "CPI inflation (% y/y)",
            gdp_yy = "Real GDP (% y/y)", unemp = "Unemployment rate (%)", hpi_yy = "House prices (% y/y)")
hh <- P$macro[P$macro$date <= date0 & P$macro$date > date0 - 365 * 3, c("date", names(mv_lab))]
hl <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(mv_lab), function(v) data.frame(date = hh$date, var = v, value = hh[[v]])))
sl <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(lib), function(k) do.call(rbind, lapply(names(mv_lab), function(v)
  data.frame(date = lib[[k]]$date, var = v, value = lib[[k]][[v]], scenario = k)))))
hl$var <- factor(mv_lab[hl$var], levels = mv_lab); sl$var <- factor(mv_lab[sl$var], levels = mv_lab)
sl$scenario <- factor(sl$scenario, levels = names(sc_col))
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = hl[is.finite(hl$value), ], aes(date, value), colour = ink[["muted"]], linewidth = 0.55) +
  geom_line(data = sl, aes(date, value, colour = scenario, linetype = scenario), linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ var, ncol = 3, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sc_col, labels = sc_short) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(baseline = "solid", upside = "solid", downside = "solid", downside_cuts = "22"),
                        labels = sc_short) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

```{r macro-twin}

  s <- lib[[k]]
  data.frame(Scenario = sc_short[[k]], `Repo, peak` = num(max(s$repo), 2), `Repo, end` = num(utils::tail(s$repo, 1), 2),

}))
```
