## What the scenarios do to the industry and to NGFB

```{r roe-dots}
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-cap: "Three-year average ROE by scenario: NGFB with its hedge, NGFB without it, and the BA900 sector through the same engine (unhedged)."
rl <- rbind(data.frame(scenario = sumtab$scenario, who = "NGFB", roe = sumtab$ngfb),
            data.frame(scenario = sumtab$scenario, who = "NGFB without hedge", roe = sumtab$ngfb_nohedge),
            data.frame(scenario = sumtab$scenario, who = "Sector (unhedged)", roe = sumtab$sector))
rl$scenario <- factor(sc_short[rl$scenario], levels = rev(sc_short))
ggplot(rl, aes(roe, scenario, colour = who)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(NGFB = ent_col[["NGFB"]], `NGFB without hedge` = "#86b6ef",
                                 `Sector (unhedged)` = ink[["secondary"]])) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(1)) +
  labs(x = "ROE, three-year average", y = NULL)
```

```{r attribution}
#| echo: false
aa <- att[att$metric %in% c("roe", "net_income"), ]
aa <- aa[order(match(aa$scenario, c("upside", "downside", "downside_cuts")), aa$entity, aa$metric == "net_income"), ]
fmt <- function(v, m) ifelse(m == "roe", bps(v), srbn(v, 1))
kt(data.frame(Scenario = sc_short[aa$scenario], Entity = aa$entity, Metric = ifelse(aa$metric == "roe", "ROE", "Net income, 3 years"),
              Volume = fmt(aa$volume, aa$metric), `Pricing (incl. hedge)` = fmt(aa$pricing, aa$metric),
              Credit = fmt(aa$credit, aa$metric), `Fees and costs` = fmt(aa$fees_costs, aa$metric),
              Interaction = fmt(aa$interaction, aa$metric), Total = fmt(aa$total, aa$metric), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lllrrrrrr", caption = "Change against the baseline, by channel: three-year average ROE and three-year net income. Each channel swaps one block of engine inputs from the scenario into the baseline run; the interaction is the residual.")
```

The industry is an **endowment play**. Without a hedge, its deposits and
capital earn more when rates rise, so in the downside the higher repo path
adds `r bps(att_r("downside", "Sector", "pricing"))` to the sector's ROE and offsets the credit
losses (`r bps(att_r("downside", "Sector", "credit"))`); in the upside the cuts take
`r bps(att_r("upside", "Sector", "pricing"))` away and the better credit picture only partly
compensates. NGFB is a **credit play**, and in this version a slightly
**liability-sensitive** one. Its unsecured-heavy book makes credit its largest channel
(`r bps(att_r("downside", "NGFB", "credit"))` in the downside, `r bps(att_r("upside", "NGFB", "credit"))` in the upside),
and its receive-fixed hedge, sized for slower deposit repricing than the
refined models now find, more than offsets its endowment: higher rates cost it
`r ubps(att_r("downside", "NGFB", "pricing"))` in the downside, and lower rates add
`r ubps(att_r("upside", "NGFB", "pricing"))` in the upside. In net income the downside
costs NGFB `r urbn(att_r("downside", m = "net_income"))` over three years
(`r urbn(-att_r("downside", "NGFB", "credit", "net_income"))` of it credit), while the sector,
`r num(sumtab["baseline", "sector_ni"] / base$ni, 1)` times NGFB's size in earnings, makes
`r srbn(att_r("downside", "Sector", m = "net_income"))`.

The **variant** shows how much rides on the policy response. With the same
contraction but rate cuts, the hedge earns `r bps(att_r("downside_cuts", "NGFB", "pricing"))` for
NGFB, which loses `r ubps(att_r("downside_cuts"))` in total, about half the stagflationary
loss, while the unhedged sector loses `r ubps(att_r("downside_cuts", "Sector"))`. A
structural hedge protects against the downturns of 2009 and 2020; it does
not protect against a downturn that comes with hikes.

The hedge also explains why NGFB's *level* of ROE sits above the sector's. In
the baseline NGFB earns `r pct(base$ngfb)` with its hedge and
`r pct(base$ngfb_nohedge)` without it: the receive-fixed book carries an average
fixed rate of `r num(SC$hedge0$fixed0, 2)`%, locked in over the past five years,
against a JIBAR path averaging `r num(mean(res$baseline$scenario$jibar3m), 2)`% over the
horizon, and new swaps are struck at a term premium over JIBAR. Unhedged, NGFB
earns less than the sector because its credit losses are higher. The carry is
the value of a position taken when rates were higher, not a free lunch: it is
what the hedge pays for giving up the upside in a hiking cycle.

```{r roe-paths}
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "NGFB's quarterly ROE and cumulative net income by scenario."
rp <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(allr), function(k) { q <- allr[[k]]$ngfb$run$quarterly
  data.frame(date = q$date, roe = q$roe, ni = cumsum(q$net_income), scenario = k) }))
rp$scenario <- factor(rp$scenario, levels = names(sc_col))
p1 <- ggplot(rp, aes(date, roe, colour = scenario, linetype = scenario)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sc_col, labels = sc_short) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(baseline = "solid", upside = "solid", downside = "solid", downside_cuts = "22"),
                        labels = sc_short) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "annualised ROE")
p2 <- ggplot(rp, aes(date, ni / 1e6, colour = scenario, linetype = scenario)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sc_col, labels = sc_short) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(baseline = "solid", upside = "solid", downside = "solid", downside_cuts = "22"),
                        labels = sc_short) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "cumulative net income (R bn)")
if (requireNamespace("patchwork", quietly = TRUE)) {
  print(patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2, ncol = 2, guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "top"))
} else print(p1)
```

```{r roe-paths-twin}

#| results: asis
rpw <- stats::reshape(data.frame(Quarter = qlab(rp$date), scenario = sc_short[as.character(rp$scenario)],
                                 v = paste0(pct(rp$roe), " / ", rbn(rp$ni, 1))),

names(rpw) <- sub("^v\\.", "", names(rpw))
twin(rpw, "Table view: quarterly ROE / cumulative net income")
```

Capital and liquidity are not the constraint in any scenario: NGFB's CET1
ratio never falls below `r pct(min(sumtab$cet1_min))` (management floor
`r pct(CFG$cet1_min)`), and its LCR proxy never below `r pct(min(sumtab$lcr_min), 0)`
(floor `r pct(CFG$lcr_min, 0)`).

## Model risk in the scenarios

```{r model-risk}
#| echo: false
kt(data.frame(Scenario = sc_short[mr$scenario], `Core ROE` = pct(mr$core),
              `Credit losses convex in a contraction` = paste0(pct(mr$convex), " (", bps(mr$convex - mr$core), ")"),
              `No intercept correction on credit losses` = paste0(pct(mr$no_ic_credit), " (", bps(mr$no_ic_credit - mr$core), ")"),
              `Core net income` = rbn(mr$core_ni, 1), `Convex: net income` = srbn(mr$convex_ni - mr$core_ni),
              `No credit correction: net income` = srbn(mr$no_ic_credit_ni - mr$core_ni), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lrrrrrr", caption = "NGFB's three-year average ROE and net income under two alternative credit models (changes against the core in brackets).")
```

Two credit-model choices deserve a flag. If losses are
convex in a contraction (the kinked model from the model checks), growth above
zero no longer lowers them, so the upside's credit benefit shrinks
(`r bps(mr["upside", "convex"] - mr["upside", "core"])` of ROE), while the downside barely changes because its
two years of negative growth produce about the same losses either way. And the
intercept correction on the credit-loss ratio, which carries the industry's
recent better-than-modelled loss experience forward, is worth
`r ubps(mr["baseline", "core"] - mr["baseline", "no_ic_credit"])` of ROE in every scenario: it moves the
level of NGFB's returns, not the differences between scenarios, and not the
positioning.

# Sensitivities {#sensitivities}

```{r sens-chart}
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-cap: "NGFB's three-year average ROE response to one-variable shocks around the baseline, by channel. The dot is the total."
sh_lab <- c(repo_up_100 = "Repo +100 bps", repo_down_100 = "Repo −100 bps", gdp_down_1 = "GDP growth −1 pp",
            unemp_up_2 = "Unemployment +2 pp", hpi_down_10 = "House prices −10% (year 1)",
            zar_weaker_10 = "Rand 10% weaker (year 1)", gov10y_up_100 = "10-year yield +100 bps",
            cpi_up_1 = "CPI +1 pp")
ch_lab <- c(volume = "Volume", pricing = "Pricing (incl. hedge)", credit = "Credit", fees_costs = "Fees and costs",
            interaction = "Interaction")
sl2 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(ch_lab), function(k) data.frame(shock = sens$shock, channel = k, v = sens[[k]])))
sl2$shock <- factor(sh_lab[sl2$shock], levels = rev(sh_lab)); sl2$channel <- factor(ch_lab[sl2$channel], levels = ch_lab)
tot <- data.frame(shock = factor(sh_lab[sens$shock], levels = rev(sh_lab)), v = sens$total)
ggplot(sl2, aes(1e4 * v, shock, fill = channel)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = tot, aes(1e4 * v, shock), inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 2.4, colour = ink[["primary"]]) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(unname(pal$categorical[1:4]), ink[["muted"]])) +
  labs(x = "change in ROE (bps)", y = NULL)
```

```{r sens-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
twin(data.frame(Shock = sh_lab[sens$shock], Total = bps(sens$total), `Net income, 3 years` = srm(sens$net_income),
                Volume = bps(sens$volume), Pricing = bps(sens$pricing), Credit = bps(sens$credit),
                `Fees and costs` = bps(sens$fees_costs), `NIM` = bps(sens$nim), `Credit-loss ratio` = bps(sens$clr),
                `CET1, end` = bps(sens$cet1_end), `Total without hedge` = bps(snh[sens$shock, "total"]), check.names = FALSE))
```

The sensitivities answer "how exposed are we" one variable at a time
(one basis point of ROE is about `r urm(bp1)` of net income a year):

* **Rates.** ±100 bps on the repo path moves NGFB's ROE by
  `r bps(sens["repo_up_100", "total"])` / `r bps(sens["repo_down_100", "total"])`
  (`r srm(sens["repo_up_100", "net_income"])` / `r srm(sens["repo_down_100", "net_income"])` of net income over three years).
  Without the hedge the same shocks would move it by
  `r bps(snh["repo_up_100", "total"])` / `r bps(snh["repo_down_100", "total"])`. The hedge,
  `r pct(hedge_ratio0)` of non-maturity deposits, was sized in Post 3 for slower
  deposit repricing than the refined Stage 1 models find, so it now more than
  neutralises the endowment and leaves NGFB modestly liability-sensitive. A
  rate rise also costs `r ubps(sens["repo_up_100", "credit"])` through credit losses.
* **Growth.** One point less GDP growth for three years costs
  `r ubps(sens["gdp_down_1", "total"])` (`r srm(sens["gdp_down_1", "net_income"])`), almost all of it
  through credit losses (`r bps(sens["gdp_down_1", "credit"])`). This is NGFB's
  largest single exposure.
* **House prices** matter through mortgage and VAF pricing and credit
  (`r bps(sens["hpi_down_10", "total"])` for a 10% fall in the first year).
* **Inflation** helps a little (`r bps(sens["cpi_up_1", "total"])` per point)
  because fee income tracks nominal activity.
* **Unemployment** has essentially no effect (`r bps(sens["unemp_up_2", "total"])`):
  no credit-loss specification with unemployment survives the sign and
  t-tests, so the engine has no unemployment channel. Unemployment is not
  harmless; the South African series is too slow-moving and too noisy, given
  GDP, to identify one.

# Positioning before the scenario arrives

## The optimisation problem

The decision is a set of balance-sheet moves made at the jump-off: transfers
of one percent of total assets from HQLA (the liquidity numeraire) into a
lending book, from wholesale funding into a deposit category, or a change in
the receive-fixed hedge of one percent of the non-maturity deposit (NMD) base.
The full engine is the source of truth; around the status quo it is close to
linear in the moves, so for every scenario $s$ the ROE gradient $G_s$ and the
gradients of the CET1 and LCR troughs and of net income come from central
finite differences.

A naive optimiser would simply maximise the engine's ROE. Even with the
execution costs below it grows every lending book out of HQLA, pushes
`r raw_up` of the six to their upper bound and claims `r ubps(raw_gain)` of
probability-weighted ROE: the engine prices new volume at the book's
*average* yield, loss rate and cost ratio, and holds equity fixed, so any risk
asset looks better than HQLA. That static attractiveness is a franchise and
capacity question (marginal pricing, cost to serve, adverse selection) that
public data cannot price. The positioning question is different: *what should
change because scenario X is coming?*

The answer used here treats the status quo as optimal under the baseline (the
balance sheet reflects the bank's central plan). That reveals an implied
marginal cost for every move, $c = G_{\text{baseline}}$, in the same way
Black and Litterman back out implied returns from market weights. Positioning
then trades on how a scenario changes each move's value:

$$ \max_x \; \sum_s w_s \big(R_s + (G_s - c)\,x\big) \;-\; \tfrac{\lambda}{2}\, \mathrm{Var}_w\!\big(R + G x\big) \;-\; \tfrac12\, x' K x $$

subject to the CET1 floor (`r pct(CFG$cet1_min)`), the LCR floor
(`r pct(CFG$lcr_min, 0)`) and move bounds, where $K$ is an execution cost:
pricing concessions and acquisition costs to grow a book within a year,
attrition to shrink it. With one scenario treated as certain ($w_X = 1$,
$\lambda = 0$) and no constraint binding, the problem separates move by move
and has a closed form:

$$ x_k^{*} = \frac{G_{X,k} - c_k}{2\,\kappa_k}, \qquad \text{net gain} = \sum_k \frac{(G_{X,k} - c_k)^2}{4\,\kappa_k}, $$

where $\kappa_k$ is the execution cost of a one-unit move. Every result is
re-run through the full engine and reported net of $c'x$ and
$\tfrac12 x'Kx$, in ROE and in net income (the implied cost in net-income
terms is the net-income gradient under the baseline, so the status quo is
optimal in both). The quadratic programme's linear prediction and the engine
agree to within `r ubps(max(abs(O$own - O$pred)), 2)` of ROE.

```{r moves-table}
#| echo: false
c0 <- O$implied_cost
short_line <- c(hqla = "HQLA", wholesale_other = "Wholesale funding")
kt(data.frame(Move = mv$label, From = ifelse(is.na(mv$from), "—", short_line[mv$from]),
              Unit = ifelse(mv$unit == "hedge", "1% of NMD", "1% of assets"),
              Bounds = sprintf("%+.1f to %+.1f", mv$lower, mv$upper),
              `Execution cost of a 1-unit move` = ubps(mv$cost, 1),
              `Engine ROE gain per unit, baseline (= implied cost)` = bps(c0, 1),
              `Net income per unit, baseline` = srm(O$implied_ni), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lllrrrr", caption = "Moves, bounds and costs. The last two columns are what the engine says each move earns under the baseline before any marginal cost (net income over three years); the optimiser treats them as the move's implied marginal cost.")
```

The hedge is bounded by policy (a hedge ratio of roughly 25–75% of NMD) and
penalised for deviating from Post 3's variance-optimal ratio rather than for
transaction costs, which are negligible for swaps.

## How the problem is solved, step by step {.steps}

For every scenario the same eight steps run, in `analysis/05_scenarios.R` and
`analysis/06_optimise.R`:

1. **Project the scenario.** The macro path drives the Stage 1 sector models
   (volumes, spreads, deposit costs, credit losses, fees, costs) and the
   Stage 2 share models (NGFB's growth relative to the sector, by regime).
2. **Run the status quo.** The engine projects NGFB's balance sheet, P&L,
   capital and liquidity quarter by quarter: ROE $R_s$, net income, CET1 and
   LCR troughs.
3. **Measure the gradients.** Each move is made at ±0.5 units and the engine
   re-run: $G_{s,k} = (\text{ROE}^{+} - \text{ROE}^{-})/1$, and likewise for
   net income, CET1 and LCR.
4. **Back out the implied costs.** $c_k = G_{\text{baseline},k}$: the plan is
   built for the baseline, so at the margin no move adds value there.
5. **Net gradient.** $G_{s,k} - c_k$ is what scenario $s$ changes about the
   value of move $k$.
6. **Solve.** The quadratic programme (`quadprog`'s dual active-set method)
   maximises net gradient times moves less execution cost, subject to the
   bounds and the CET1 and LCR floors. When nothing binds the solution is the
   closed form above, one line per move.
7. **Re-run and bridge.** The engine is re-run with the moves, which captures
   everything the linear model misses (moves compound with growth, equity
   builds); each move's contribution is measured sequentially, net of its
   implied and execution cost, so the bars add up to the total.
8. **Score the alternatives.** The same moves are evaluated under every other
   scenario: the cost of being wrong.

## The baseline: what NGFB does in its plan

```{r plan}
#| echo: false
qb <- res$baseline$ngfb$run$quarterly
yr <- rep(seq_len(yrs), each = 4)
ag <- function(v, f = sum) as.numeric(tapply(qb[[v]], yr, f))
lastq <- function(x) utils::tail(x, 1)
plan <- data.frame(
  Item = c("Total assets, year end", "Loans, year end", "Deposits, year end", "Net interest income",
           "of which hedge carry", "Non-interest revenue", "Operating costs", "Credit impairments",
           "Profit before tax", "Net income", "ROE (average)", "NIM (average)", "Credit-loss ratio (average)",
           "CET1 ratio, year end", "LCR, trough"),
  rbind(num(ag("total_assets", lastq) / 1e6, 0), num(ag("loans", lastq) / 1e6, 0), num(ag("deposits", lastq) / 1e6, 0),
        num(ag("nii") / 1e6, 1), num(ag("hedge_pl") / 1e6, 1), num(ag("nir") / 1e6, 1), num(ag("opex") / 1e6, 1),
        num(ag("impairments") / 1e6, 1), num(ag("pbt") / 1e6, 1), num(ag("net_income") / 1e6, 1),
        pct(ag("roe", mean)), pct(ag("nim", mean), 2), pct(ag("clr", mean), 2), pct(ag("cet1_ratio", lastq)),
        pct(ag("lcr", min), 0)), check.names = FALSE)
names(plan)[-1] <- paste0("Year ", seq_len(yrs), " (to ", qlab(qb$date[4 * seq_len(yrs)]), ")")
kt(plan, align = paste0("l", strrep("r", yrs)),
   caption = "NGFB's baseline plan by year. Amounts in R bn; flows are annual totals.")
ta_g <- (ag("total_assets", lastq)[yrs] / ta0)^(1 / yrs) - 1
guard(all(diff(ag("roe", mean)) > 0) && all(diff(ag("cet1_ratio", lastq)) > 0), "plan: ROE and CET1 rise each year")
sw5 <- res$baseline$scenario$swap5y; jb <- res$baseline$scenario$jibar3m
book_end <- (sum(rep(SC$hedge0$fixed0, 20L - length(sw5))) + sum(sw5)) / 20
guard(book_end < SC$hedge0$fixed0 && (SC$hedge0$fixed0 - book_end) < (jb[1] - utils::tail(jb, 1)) &&
      all(diff(ag("hedge_pl")) > 0), "hedge book drifts down slower than JIBAR, carry grows")
```

In the baseline NGFB does not reposition; it runs its plan. The balance sheet
grows about `r pct(ta_g, 0)` a year, the sector's projected growth plus NGFB's
regime-dependent share dynamics, line by line. Loans reprice with prime and
JIBAR plus the sector's projected spreads; deposits reprice with the
Stage 1 deposit costs. One twentieth of the receive-fixed hedge rolls off
every quarter and is replaced at the then five-year swap rate, so the hedge's
average fixed rate drifts down slowly from `r num(SC$hedge0$fixed0, 2)`% while
JIBAR falls faster, and the hedge carry grows from `r rbn(ag("hedge_pl")[1], 1)` in year one to
`r rbn(ag("hedge_pl")[yrs], 1)` in year three. Credit losses follow the sector's
loss ratio scaled by NGFB's product mix (`r pct(base$clr, 2)` of loans against the
sector's `r pct(base$sector_clr, 2)`); fees and costs follow the sector's ratios to
assets. Half of net income is paid out, so CET1 builds from
`r pct(q0$cet1_ratio[1])` to `r pct(lastq(qb$cet1_ratio))` and ROE rises each year as the
margin widens with the easing cycle, from `r pct(ag("roe", mean)[1])` to
`r pct(ag("roe", mean)[yrs])`. The positioning for the baseline is zero by
construction: the plan is optimal for the scenario it was built for.

```{r walk-helpers}
#| include: false
gr_ann <- function(r, who) colMeans(400 * log(r[[who]]$inputs$growth[, -1, drop = FALSE]))
ind_tab <- function(s) {
  pb <- res$baseline$ngfb$proj; ps <- allr[[s]]$ngfb$proj
  v <- c(g_mortgages_res = "Residential mortgages, growth (% a year)", g_cards = "Credit cards, growth",
         g_personal_other = "Personal loans, growth", g_corp_all = "Corporate loans, growth",
         g_nmd = "Non-maturity deposits, growth", clr = "Credit-loss ratio (% of loans)",
         c_current = "Cost of current accounts (%)", c_savings = "Cost of savings deposits (%)",
         c_fixed_notice = "Cost of fixed and notice deposits (%)", s_homeloans = "Home-loan yield less prime (pp)",
         s_cards = "Card yield less prime (pp)", nir_assets = "Non-interest revenue (% of assets)")
  b <- colMeans(pb[, names(v)]); x <- colMeans(ps[, names(v)])
  data.frame(`Industry (Stage 1), three-year average` = v, Baseline = num(b, 2), Scenario = num(x, 2),
             Change = sprintf("%+.2f", x - b), check.names = FALSE)
}
share_tab <- function(s) {
  r <- allr[[s]]; rb <- res$baseline
  lines_ <- c(cards = "Credit cards", personal_other = "Personal loans", vaf = "Vehicle and asset finance",
              mortgages_res = "Residential mortgages", corporate_loans = "Corporate loans", beh_savings = "Non-maturity deposits")
  ng <- gr_ann(r, "ngfb")[names(lines_)]; se <- gr_ann(r, "sector")[names(lines_)]
  ngb <- gr_ann(rb, "ngfb")[names(lines_)]; seb <- gr_ann(rb, "sector")[names(lines_)]
  data.frame(`Line` = lines_, `Sector growth` = num(se, 1), `NGFB growth` = num(ng, 1),
             `NGFB share change (pp of growth)` = sprintf("%+.1f", ng - se),
             `Same, in the baseline` = sprintf("%+.1f", ngb - seb), check.names = FALSE)
}
walk_tab <- function(s) {
  w <- O$walk[[s]]
  f1 <- function(x) sprintf("%+.1f", 1e4 * x)
  data.frame(Move = w$label, `G: engine gain per unit (bps)` = f1(w$g), `c: implied cost (bps)` = f1(w$c),
             `G - c (bps)` = f1(w$net), `Execution cost (bps)` = sprintf("%.1f", 1e4 * w$cost),
             `Move = (G - c) / 2 cost` = sprintf("%+.2f", w$x_unc), `Bounds` = sprintf("%+.1f%s%+.1f", w$lower, "\u00a0to\u00a0", w$upper),
             `Contribution: ROE (bps)` = f1(w$engine), `Contribution: net income (R m)` = sprintf("%+.0f", w$engine_ni / 1e3),
             check.names = FALSE)
}
regs_of <- function(s) { t <- table(factor(allr[[s]]$ngfb$regimes$regime, levels = c("contraction", "hiking", "easing", "neutral")))
  paste(sprintf("%d %s", t[t > 0], names(t)[t > 0]), collapse = ", ") }
bridge_plot <- function(X) {
  br <- O$bridges[[X]]$bridge
  sc_steps <- br[br$kind == "scenario", ]; po_steps <- br[br$kind == "positioning", ]
  big <- abs(po_steps$roe) >= 0.5e-4
  po2 <- po_steps[big, c("step", "roe")]
  if (any(!big)) po2 <- rbind(po2, data.frame(step = "Smaller moves", roe = sum(po_steps$roe[!big])))
  mid <- br$roe[1] + sum(sc_steps$roe)
  guard(abs(mid - sumtab[X, "ngfb"]) < 1e-10, "bridge does not pass through the scenario's ROE")
  wf <- rbind(data.frame(step = br$step[1], kind = "level", v = br$roe[1]),
              data.frame(step = sc_steps$step, kind = "step", v = sc_steps$roe),
              data.frame(step = sprintf("%s, unpositioned", sc_short[[X]]), kind = "level", v = mid),
              data.frame(step = po2$step, kind = "step", v = po2$roe),
              data.frame(step = br$step[nrow(br)], kind = "level", v = br$roe[nrow(br)]))
  cur <- 0; wf$start <- NA_real_; wf$end <- NA_real_
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(wf))) {
    if (wf$kind[i] == "level") { wf$start[i] <- wf$end[i] <- wf$v[i]; cur <- wf$v[i] }
    else { wf$start[i] <- cur; wf$end[i] <- cur + wf$v[i]; cur <- wf$end[i] }
  }
  guard(abs(cur - wf$v[nrow(wf)]) < 1e-10, "waterfall does not close")
  wf$id <- seq_len(nrow(wf))
  wf$dir <- ifelse(wf$kind == "level", "level", ifelse(wf$v >= 0, "up", "down"))
  wf$lab <- ifelse(wf$kind == "level", pct(wf$v, 2), bps(wf$v))
  lo <- min(c(wf$start, wf$end)); hi <- max(c(wf$start, wf$end))
  ggplot(wf) +
    geom_rect(data = wf[wf$kind == "step", ],
              aes(xmin = id - 0.32, xmax = id + 0.32, ymin = pmin(start, end), ymax = pmax(start, end), fill = dir)) +
    geom_segment(data = wf[wf$kind == "level", ], aes(x = id - 0.38, xend = id + 0.38, y = v, yend = v),
                 colour = ink[["primary"]], linewidth = 1.1) +
    geom_segment(data = wf[-nrow(wf), ], aes(x = id + 0.32, xend = id + 0.68, y = end, yend = end),
                 colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_text(aes(x = id, y = pmax(start, end), label = lab), vjust = -0.7, size = 3, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(up = div_hi, down = div_lo), guide = "none") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = wf$id, labels = wf$step) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(0.1), limits = c(lo - 0.15 * (hi - lo), hi + 0.2 * (hi - lo))) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "ROE, three-year average") +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
}
bridge_twin <- function(X) {
  br <- O$bridges[[X]]$bridge
  twin(data.frame(Step = br$step, Kind = br$kind, `ROE` = ifelse(br$kind == "level", pct(br$roe, 2), bps(br$roe, 1)),
                  `Net income, 3 years` = ifelse(br$kind == "level", rbn(br$ni, 1), srm(br$ni)),
                  `NIM-equivalent` = ifelse(br$kind == "level", sprintf("%.0f bps", br$nim_eq_bps), sprintf("%+.1f bps", br$nim_eq_bps)),
                  check.names = FALSE),
       sprintf("Table view (1 bp of NIM-equivalent, pre-tax profit over interest-earning assets, = %.1f bps of ROE)", O$m_conv))
}
wD <- O$walk$downside; wU <- O$walk$upside
gD <- function(m, v = "engine") wD[[v]][wD$move == m]; gU <- function(m, v = "engine") wU[[v]][wU$move == m]
ld <- lib$downside; lb <- lib$baseline; lu <- lib$upside
guard(gD("hedge") > 0.5 * rg$gain["downside", "downside"], "the hedge is most of the downside positioning")
guard(gU("hedge") > 0.5 * rg$gain["upside", "upside"], "the hedge is most of the upside positioning")
```

## The downside, step by step

**1. The macro path.** The repo rate rises from the baseline's
`r num(max(lb$repo), 2)`% peak to `r num(max(ld$repo), 2)`% by `r qlab(ld$date[which.max(ld$repo)])`,
inflation peaks at `r num(max(ld$cpi_yy), 1)`%, the long bond at `r num(max(ld$gov10y), 2)`%,
and real GDP contracts for `r sum(ld$gdp_yy < 0)` quarters, troughing at
`r num(min(ld$gdp_yy), 1)`% year on year; unemployment peaks at `r num(max(ld$unemp), 1)`%
and house prices fall.

**2. What the industry does (Stage 1).**

```{r down-industry}
#| echo: false
kt(ind_tab("downside"), align = "lrrr", caption = "The sector's projected paths in the downside against the baseline.")
```

The sector's credit-loss ratio rises by `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(allr$downside$ngfb$proj$clr) - mean(res$baseline$ngfb$proj$clr))`
pp, deposit costs follow the repo rate up (savings by `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(allr$downside$ngfb$proj$c_savings) - mean(res$baseline$ngfb$proj$c_savings))`
pp), and loan and deposit growth slow.

**3. What NGFB's share does (Stage 2).** The downside has `r regs_of("downside")`
quarters. In contractions NGFB gains card share (as the Challengers do) and
loses personal-loan and vehicle-finance share:

```{r down-share}
#| echo: false
gdn <- gr_ann(allr$downside, "ngfb"); gds <- gr_ann(allr$downside, "sector")
guard(gdn[["cards"]] > gds[["cards"]] && gdn[["personal_other"]] < gds[["personal_other"]] && gdn[["vaf"]] < gds[["vaf"]],
      "downside share claims")
guard(all(xc[c("into_mortgages", "into_vaf", "into_cards", "into_personal")] < 0) &&
      all(xc[c("fund_term", "fund_savings", "fund_operational")] < 0) &&
      abs(xc[["into_personal"]]) > abs(xc[["into_mortgages"]]), "downside-with-cuts positioning claims")
kt(share_tab("downside"), align = "lrrrr", caption = "Annualised growth over three years, percent: the sector and NGFB (Stage 2 share dynamics, drift switched off).")
```

**4. NGFB without positioning.** ROE falls to `r pct(sumtab["downside", "ngfb"])`
(`r bps(att_r("downside"))`) and net income to `r rbn(sumtab["downside", "ni"], 1)`
over three years (`r srbn(att_r("downside", m = "net_income"))`): credit
`r bps(att_r("downside", "NGFB", "credit"))`, pricing and hedge `r bps(att_r("downside", "NGFB", "pricing"))`,
volumes, fees and costs close to zero.

**5–6. Gradients, implied costs and the solution.**

```{r down-walk}
#| echo: false
kt(walk_tab("downside"), align = "lrrrrrrrr",
   caption = "The downside positioning, move by move. Moves in percent of total assets (hedge: percent of NMD); G and c in basis points of ROE per unit of move; execution cost in basis points of ROE for a one-unit move (quadratic in the move). Contributions are full-engine, sequential and net of implied and execution cost, and add up to the total gain; for very small moves ROE and net income can differ in sign, because a move shifts profit between quarters while equity grows.")
```

Reading across a row gives the whole optimisation for that move. Take the
hedge: under the baseline, one more point of hedge earns `r bps(gD("hedge", "c"), 1)` of
ROE, so that is its implied cost; under the downside it earns only
`r bps(gD("hedge", "g"), 1)`, because the floating leg it pays reprices up with
the hikes. The net gradient is `r bps(gD("hedge", "net"), 1)` a point, the execution
cost `r ubps(mv$cost[mv$move == "hedge"], 1)` a point squared, so the optimum is
(`r sprintf("%.2f", 1e4 * gD("hedge", "net"))` bps) / (2 × `r sprintf("%.2f", 1e4 * mv$cost[mv$move == "hedge"])` bps)
= `r sprintf("%+.1f", gD("hedge", "x"))` points of NMD, from `r pct(hedge_ratio0)` to
`r pct(hedge_ratio0 + posD[["hedge"]] / 100)`. Deposits gain value
(their cost lags the policy rate), so wholesale funding is swapped for savings
and transactional deposits; unsecured lending loses value (losses rise), so
cards and personal loans are trimmed; secured lending gains slightly, because
its losses rise little and its yield follows the full rise in prime, while
HQLA, `r pct(1 - gv("HQLA earning share"), 0)` of which earns nothing, captures only part of it. No bound or floor binds: the CET1 trough moves by
`r bps(sum(wD$d_cet1), 1)` and the LCR trough by `r sprintf("%+.1f points", 100 * sum(wD$d_lcr))`.

**7. Re-run and bridge.**

```{r down-bridge}
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-cap: "From the baseline plan to the downside, then to the downside positioned for it: three-year average ROE. Levels are marked with a bar; steps are labelled in basis points of ROE."
bridge_plot("downside")
```

```{r down-bridge-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
bridge_twin("downside")
```

Positioned, NGFB's ROE in the downside is `r pct(rg$roe["downside", "downside"])`:
`r bps(rg$gain["downside", "downside"])` better than unpositioned, or
`r srm(rg$gain_ni["downside", "downside"])` of net income over three years, of
which the hedge contributes `r bps(gD("hedge"))`. That recovers
`r pct(rg$gain["downside", "downside"] / abs(att_r("downside")), 0)` of the downside's
`r ubps(att_r("downside"))` hit: positioning cannot undo a credit cycle inside a
year, and the bridge makes that visible, since the largest bar is credit and
only the small unsecured trims are aimed at it.

**8. If the downside does not come.** The same moves cost
`r ubps(rg$gain["downside", "baseline"])` (`r srm(rg$gain_ni["downside", "baseline"])`) if the baseline
arrives instead and `r ubps(rg$gain["downside", "upside"])` (`r srm(rg$gain_ni["downside", "upside"])`)
if the upside does.

**And if the SARB cuts instead?** In the variant with the same contraction but
150 bps of cuts, the optimal positioning reverses the hedge
(`r sprintf("%+.1f", xc[["hedge"]])` points of NMD instead of `r sprintf("%+.1f", posD[["hedge"]])`),
shrinks deposits instead of growing them, and cuts every retail book,
unsecured most (cards `r sprintf("%+.2f", xc[["into_cards"]])`, personal loans
`r sprintf("%+.2f", xc[["into_personal"]])`). Positioning for the stagflationary
downside when the cuts arrive costs
`r ubps(O$cuts$value$pos_down[O$cuts$value$realised == "downside_cuts"])`; positioning for the cuts when
the hikes arrive costs `r ubps(O$cuts$value$pos_cuts[O$cuts$value$realised == "downside"])`. The
credit leg of a downside positioning is robust to the policy response; the
rate leg is a bet on it.

## The upside, step by step

**1. The macro path.** Inflation returns to the target sooner, the repo rate
falls to `r num(min(lu$repo), 2)`% (`r sprintf("%.2f", abs(min(lu$repo) - min(lb$repo)))` pp below
the baseline's trough), growth averages `r num(mean(lu$gdp_yy), 1)`% and house prices
`r num(mean(lu$hpi_yy), 1)`% a year.

**2–3. The industry and NGFB's share.**

```{r up-industry}
#| echo: false
kt(ind_tab("upside"), align = "lrrr", caption = "The sector's projected paths in the upside against the baseline.")
kt(share_tab("upside"), align = "lrrrr", caption = "Annualised growth over three years, percent, in the upside.")
```

The upside has `r regs_of("upside")` quarters. Lower rates cut deposit costs,
credit losses fall by `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(res$baseline$ngfb$proj$clr) - mean(allr$upside$ngfb$proj$clr))` pp of loans
and volumes grow faster.

**4. NGFB without positioning.** ROE rises to `r pct(sumtab["upside", "ngfb"])`
(`r bps(att_r("upside"))`) and net income to `r rbn(sumtab["upside", "ni"], 1)`
(`r srbn(att_r("upside", m = "net_income"))`): credit `r bps(att_r("upside", "NGFB", "credit"))`, pricing and
hedge `r bps(att_r("upside", "NGFB", "pricing"))`.

**5–6. Gradients and the solution.**

```{r up-walk}
#| echo: false
kt(walk_tab("upside"), align = "lrrrrrrrr", caption = "The upside positioning, move by move (units and conventions as for the downside).")
```

The rows mirror the downside's. The hedge is worth more than under the
baseline (`r bps(gU("hedge", "g"), 1)` against `r bps(gU("hedge", "c"), 1)` a point), because
its floating leg reprices down, so it is extended by `r sprintf("%.1f", gU("hedge", "x"))` points,
to `r pct(hedge_ratio0 + posU[["hedge"]] / 100)` of NMD. Deposits are worth less as rates
fall, so the bank lets `r pct(-(posU[["fund_savings"]] + posU[["fund_operational"]]) / 100, 2)` of assets
of savings and transactional deposits go and funds with wholesale money; better
credit makes unsecured lending worth more, so personal loans and cards grow
by `r pct((posU[["into_personal"]] + posU[["into_cards"]]) / 100, 2)` of assets. Again no bound or floor binds.

**7–8. Re-run, bridge and the cost of being wrong.**

```{r up-bridge}
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-cap: "From the baseline plan to the upside, then to the upside positioned for it: three-year average ROE."
bridge_plot("upside")
```

```{r up-bridge-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
bridge_twin("upside")
```

Positioned, NGFB earns `r pct(rg$roe["upside", "upside"])` in the upside,
`r bps(rg$gain["upside", "upside"])` more (`r srm(rg$gain_ni["upside", "upside"])` of net income).
The same moves cost `r ubps(rg$gain["upside", "baseline"])` if the baseline arrives and
`r ubps(rg$gain["upside", "downside"])` (`r srm(rg$gain_ni["upside", "downside"])`) if the downside does.

## The cost of being wrong

```{r regret}
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-cap: "Regret: ROE given up (bps) by positioning for the scenario in the row when the scenario in the column arrives, against the best positioning for that column. Net of implied and execution costs, full engine."
rgm <- rg$regret
rl3 <- expand.grid(pos = rownames(rgm), real = colnames(rgm), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
rl3$v <- 1e4 * rgm[cbind(rl3$pos, rl3$real)]
rl3$ni <- rg$regret_ni[cbind(rl3$pos, rl3$real)]
rl3$pos <- factor(sc_short[rl3$pos], levels = rev(sc_short[scen])); rl3$real <- factor(sc_short[rl3$real], levels = sc_short[scen])
ggplot(rl3, aes(real, pos, fill = v)) +
  geom_tile(colour = ink[["surface"]], linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.0f bps\n%s", v, urm(ni)), colour = v > 0.55 * max(v)), size = 3.1, lineheight = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = ink[["primary"]], `TRUE` = "#ffffff"), guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = seq_ramp, name = "bps") +
  labs(x = "scenario that arrives", y = "positioned for") +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank())
```

The regret matrix is the honest companion to every positioning. The status
quo's worst regret is `r ubps(max(rgm["baseline", ]))` (if the downside arrives);
positioning for the downside and getting the upside instead costs
`r ubps(rgm["downside", "upside"])` (`r urm(rg$regret_ni["downside", "upside"])` of net income), and the
reverse `r ubps(rgm["upside", "downside"])`. The two positionings are opposite bets on the
same levers, so being wrong costs
`r num(-rg$gain["downside", "upside"] / rg$gain["downside", "downside"], 1)` times what being right earns for the
downside positioning and `r num(-rg$gain["upside", "downside"] / rg$gain["upside", "upside"], 1)` times for the upside's.

## When there is no strong view

```{r ladder}
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-cap: "Positioning for the downside as conviction rises: the expected ROE gain (probability-weighted, net) and the gain or cost if the downside, the baseline or the upside arrives."
ldd <- O$ladders$downside
ldd$prob <- (1 - ldd$p) * O$weights[["downside"]] + ldd$p
ll <- rbind(data.frame(p = ldd$prob, what = "If the downside arrives", v = ldd$gain_if_x),
            data.frame(p = ldd$prob, what = "Expected", v = ldd$exp_gain),
            data.frame(p = ldd$prob, what = "If the baseline arrives", v = ldd$gain_if_base),
            data.frame(p = ldd$prob, what = "If the upside arrives", v = ldd$gain_if_other))
ll$what <- factor(ll$what, levels = c("If the downside arrives", "Expected", "If the baseline arrives", "If the upside arrives"))
ggplot(ll, aes(p, 1e4 * v, colour = what)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) + geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`If the downside arrives` = sc_col[["downside"]], Expected = ink[["primary"]],
                                 `If the baseline arrives` = sc_col[["baseline"]], `If the upside arrives` = sc_col[["upside"]])) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(1)) +
  labs(x = "probability attached to the downside", y = "ROE gain (bps)") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

```{r ladder-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
twin(data.frame(`P(downside)` = pct(ldd$prob, 0), `Hedge, % of NMD` = sprintf("%+.1f", ldd$hedge),
                `Unsecured lending, % of assets` = sprintf("%+.2f", ldd$into_cards + ldd$into_personal),
                `Retail deposits, % of assets` = sprintf("%+.2f", ldd$fund_savings + ldd$fund_operational),
                `Expected gain` = bps(ldd$exp_gain, 1), `If downside` = bps(ldd$gain_if_x, 1),
                `If baseline` = bps(ldd$gain_if_base, 1), `If upside` = bps(ldd$gain_if_other, 1), check.names = FALSE))
rb <- O$robust$x
guard(max(abs(rb[1:9])) < 0.1 && rb[["hedge"]] < 0, "robust positioning claims")
i65 <- which.min(abs(ldd$prob - 0.65)); sh65 <- ldd$hedge[i65] / utils::tail(ldd$hedge, 1)
```

With the scenario probabilities used here (baseline `r pct(CFG$scenario_weights[["baseline"]], 0)`,
downside `r pct(CFG$scenario_weights[["downside"]], 0)`, upside `r pct(CFG$scenario_weights[["upside"]], 0)`),
the probability-weighted positioning with variance aversion $\lambda = `r O$lambda[2]`$
moves the hedge by `r sprintf("%+.1f", rb[["hedge"]])` points of NMD and every other line
by less than `r pct(max(abs(rb[1:9])) / 100, 2)` of assets. The downside skew tilts it
slightly defensive, but the upside and downside largely cancel, and when the
bank does not know which is coming the best response is close to the plan.
The framework's value is in the other direction: it tells the ALCO what to
do, and what it costs if wrong, **as conviction about a scenario builds**.
Positioning scales almost linearly with conviction until a bound binds: at a
`r pct(ldd$prob[i65], 0)` probability of the downside the moves are about `r pct(sh65, 0)` of
the full-conviction positioning.

## More aggressive?

```{r aggr-setup}
#| include: false
agD <- O$aggressiveness$downside; agU <- O$aggressiveness$upside
szD <- agD$size; cpD <- agD$capacity; szU <- agU$size; cpU <- agU$capacity
g_at <- function(d, a, r, col = "gain") d[[col]][d$alpha == a & d$realised == r]
c_at <- function(d, k, b, r, col = "gain") d[[col]][d$cost_scale == k & d$bound_scale == b & d$realised == r]
guard(abs(g_at(szD, 2, "downside")) < 0.0001 && g_at(szD, 2, "upside") < 2 * g_at(szD, 1, "upside"),
      "size dial: doubling gives back the gain and more than doubles the loss if wrong")
guard(grepl("lower:hedge", cpD$binding[cpD$cost_scale == 0.25 & cpD$bound_scale == 1][1]), "hedge bound binds at a quarter of the cost")
guard(all(cpD$cet1_min > CFG$cet1_min + 0.005) && all(cpD$lcr_min > CFG$lcr_min + 0.3), "floors never bind")
guard(all(szD$exp_gain < 0), "full-conviction positioning has negative expected value at every size")
guard(c_at(cpD, 0.1, 2, "downside", "hedge") <= -100 * hedge_ratio0, "a tenth of the cost and doubled bounds removes the hedge")
lin_max <- max(abs(c(cpD$lin_gap, cpU$lin_gap)))
lin_mod <- max(abs(c(cpD$lin_gap[cpD$cost_scale >= 0.25 & cpD$bound_scale == 1],
                     cpU$lin_gap[cpU$cost_scale >= 0.25 & cpU$bound_scale == 1])))
guard(lin_mod < 0.0005, "the linear model is close to the engine for moderate settings")
```

Being more aggressive does move the numbers more, in both directions, and how
much depends on what "more aggressive" means. There are two different dials.

**Bigger moves at the same cost.** Take the optimal downside positioning and
scale it by a factor $\alpha$. The benefit if the downside arrives grows in
proportion to $\alpha$, but the execution cost grows with its square, so the
net gain is $(2\alpha - \alpha^2)$ times the optimum's: it peaks at the
optimum, is gone at twice the optimal size, and turns negative beyond. The
loss if the scenario does not arrive keeps growing all the while.

```{r aggr-size}
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-cap: "Scaling the optimal downside positioning up and down at the same execution cost: net ROE gain if each scenario arrives, and the probability-weighted expectation."
sz <- szD
sl3 <- rbind(data.frame(alpha = sz$alpha, what = paste("If the", sz$realised, "arrives"), v = sz$gain),
             unique(data.frame(alpha = sz$alpha, what = "Expected", v = sz$exp_gain)))
sl3$what <- factor(sl3$what, levels = c("If the downside arrives", "Expected", "If the baseline arrives", "If the upside arrives"))
ggplot(sl3, aes(alpha, 1e4 * v, colour = what)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "22") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) + geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`If the downside arrives` = sc_col[["downside"]], Expected = ink[["primary"]],
                                 `If the baseline arrives` = sc_col[["baseline"]], `If the upside arrives` = sc_col[["upside"]])) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = unique(sz$alpha), labels = paste0(unique(sz$alpha), "×")) +
  labs(x = "size of the positioning relative to the optimum", y = "net ROE gain (bps)") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

```{r aggr-size-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
st <- stats::reshape(data.frame(alpha = paste0(sz$alpha, "×"), r = sz$realised, v = paste0(bps(sz$gain), " / ", srm(sz$gain_ni))),
                     idvar = "alpha", timevar = "r", direction = "wide")
names(st) <- c("Size", paste("If", sub("^v\\.", "", names(st)[-1]), "arrives (ROE / net income)"))
st$Hedge <- sprintf("%+.1f", unique(sz[, c("alpha", "hedge")])$hedge)
twin(st, "Table view: net gain by size of the downside positioning")
```

**A bank that can move faster or more cheaply.** A bank with spare deposit
franchise, an underwriting machine ready to scale, or a longer runway can
execute the same moves for less. The optimiser then chooses bigger moves:
halve the execution costs and the moves, the gain if right and the loss if
wrong all double, until a bound binds.

```{r aggr-capacity}
#| echo: false
bind_lab <- c(hedge = "hedge", into_cards = "cards", into_personal = "personal loans", into_cre = "commercial property",
              fund_savings = "savings", fund_operational = "transactional", into_mortgages = "mortgages",
              into_vaf = "VAF", into_corporate = "corporate", fund_term = "term deposits")
binds <- function(b) { if (!nchar(b)) return("nothing")
  k <- sub("^(lower|upper):", "", strsplit(b, "; ")[[1]]); paste(unique(bind_lab[k]), collapse = ", ") }
cp <- cpD[cpD$cost_scale <= 1 & (cpD$bound_scale == 1 | cpD$cost_scale <= 0.25), ]
cpw <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(cp, list(cp$cost_scale, cp$bound_scale), drop = TRUE), function(z) {
  g <- function(r, col = "gain") z[[col]][z$realised == r]
  data.frame(cost = z$cost_scale[1], bounds = z$bound_scale[1],
             `Execution cost` = paste0(z$cost_scale[1], "×"), Bounds = ifelse(z$bound_scale[1] == 1, "as set", "doubled"),
             `Hedge (pp of NMD)` = sprintf("%+.1f", z$hedge[1]),
             `Unsecured lending (% of assets)` = sprintf("%+.2f", z$into_cards[1] + z$into_personal[1]),
             `Retail deposits (% of assets)` = sprintf("%+.2f", z$fund_savings[1] + z$fund_operational[1]),
             `If downside (bps)` = sprintf("%+.0f", 1e4 * g("downside")), `If baseline (bps)` = sprintf("%+.0f", 1e4 * g("baseline")),
             `If upside (bps)` = sprintf("%+.0f", 1e4 * g("upside")), `Expected (bps)` = sprintf("%+.1f", 1e4 * z$exp_gain[1]),
             `If downside (R m)` = sprintf("%+.0f", g("downside", "gain_ni") / 1e3), `If upside (R m)` = sprintf("%+.0f", g("upside", "gain_ni") / 1e3),
             `At a bound` = binds(z$binding[1]), check.names = FALSE)
}))
cpw <- cpw[order(cpw$bounds, -cpw$cost), ]
kt(cpw[, c(3:11, 14)], align = "llrrrrrrrl",
   caption = "Positioning for the downside when execution is cheaper (and, in the last rows, the bounds are doubled, so the hedge may go from 0% to 100% of NMD): the moves and the net ROE gain if each scenario arrives.")
```

```{r aggr-capacity-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
twin(cpw[, c(3, 4, 12, 13)], "Table view: the same in net income over three years")
```

At a quarter of the cost, the hedge hits its policy floor and the downside
positioning earns `r bps(c_at(cpD, 0.25, 1, "downside"))` (`r srm(c_at(cpD, 0.25, 1, "downside", "gain_ni"))`) if the
downside comes, but loses `r ubps(c_at(cpD, 0.25, 1, "upside"))` (`r srm(c_at(cpD, 0.25, 1, "upside", "gain_ni"))`)
if the upside comes. With a tenth of the cost and doubled bounds, which means
taking the hedge off entirely, the numbers become
`r bps(c_at(cpD, 0.1, 2, "downside"))` against `r bps(c_at(cpD, 0.1, 2, "upside"))`. The same pattern holds for the
upside positioning (`r bps(c_at(cpU, 0.25, 1, "upside"))` if right, `r bps(c_at(cpU, 0.25, 1, "downside"))` if the
downside arrives, at a quarter of the cost).

Three things stop aggressiveness from being free:

* **The loss if wrong grows faster than the gain if right.** The upside and
  the downside move the same levers in opposite directions, so a bigger
  downside bet loses more in the upside than it makes in the downside, and with
  a `r pct(CFG$scenario_weights[["downside"]], 0)` chance of the downside the probability-weighted
  value of full-conviction positioning is negative at every size
  (`r bps(g_at(szD, 1, "downside", "exp_gain"), 1)` at the optimum); the probability-weighted
positioning in the previous section is the one that adds value on average.
* **Bounds bind before capital or liquidity do.** Even the most aggressive
  setting leaves the CET1 trough above `r pct(min(cpD$cet1_min))` and the LCR trough
  above `r pct(min(cpD$lcr_min), 0)`; what stops the moves is the hedge policy and
  the speed at which a franchise can grow or shrink a book.
* **The answer is only as good as the costs.** The execution costs are
  assumptions about franchise capacity, and the size of every lending move
  scales with them. Their direction does not depend on them; their size does.

The optimiser's linear model stays close to the full engine for moderate
settings (within `r ubps(lin_mod, 2)` of ROE down to a quarter of the cost) but
drifts at the extremes (up to `r ubps(lin_max, 1)` when the bounds are doubled and
the hedge is pushed towards 0% or 100% of NMD), which is why every number
above is the full engine's, not the linear model's.

# Market share and market growth: where NGFB should lean in {#share-strategy}

```{r strat-setup}
#| include: false
ST <- rd("strategy.rds"); PF <- rd("performance.rds")
pos <- ST$positioning; val <- ST$value; mg <- ST$margins; gn <- ST$gainers
cell <- function(p, r) pos[pos$product == p & pos$regime == r, ]
mk_g <- function(p, r) ST$market$growth[ST$market$product == p & ST$market$regime == r]
mk_avg <- function(p) ST$market$mean_all[ST$market$product == p][1]
gain_to <- function(p, r, to) { x <- gn[gn$product == p & gn$regime == r & gn$to == to, "share_of_loss"]; if (length(x)) x else 0 }
vv <- function(p, r, s, to = "par", f = "wholesale", col = "contribution")
  val[val$product == p & val$regime == r & val$scenario == s & val$to == to & val$funding == f, col]
hm <- function(p, s = "baseline", f = "wholesale")
  mean(mg$headroom[mg$product == p & mg$scenario == s & mg$funding == f])
## every claim in this chapter
ce <- cell("cards", "easing"); co <- cell("corp_all", "easing"); ve <- cell("vaf", "easing")
cc <- cell("cards", "contraction"); ch <- cell("cards", "hiking"); pc <- cell("personal_other", "contraction")
th <- cell("beh_term", "hiking"); vc <- cell("vaf", "contraction"); ph <- cell("personal_other", "hiking")
guard(ce$action == "Push" && co$action == "Push" && ve$action == "Push", "easing pushes")
guard(mk_g("cards", "easing") > mk_avg("cards") && ce$ngfb_effect < 0 && ce$par < 0, "cards in easing")
guard(gain_to("cards", "easing", "Challengers") > 0.9, "the Challengers take NGFB's card share in easing")
guard(cc$action == "Guard" && cc$ngfb_effect > 0 && mk_g("cards", "contraction") < 1, "cards in contraction")
guard(ch$action == "Ride" && ch$ngfb_effect > 0, "cards in hiking")
guard(pc$action == "Let go" && th$action == "Defend" && vc$action == "Defend" && ph$action == "Guard", "other actions")
guard(hm("cards") > 1 && hm("corp_all") > 0.5 && hm("corp_all") < 1.2 && hm("vaf") < 0.25 && hm("vaf") > -0.1,
      "wholesale headroom ordering")
guard(hm("corp_all", f = "blended") > 2.5 && hm("vaf", f = "blended") > 2, "blended headroom")
guard(mean(mg$headroom[mg$product == "vaf" & mg$scenario == "downside" & mg$funding == "wholesale"]) < 0,
      "VAF does not pay on wholesale funding in the downside")
guard(vv("cards", "contraction", "downside") < 0, "giving up the downside card share loses contribution at average losses")
pb <- ST$playbook
pbv <- function(s, f, col = "contribution") pb[pb$scenario == s & pb$funding == f, col]
guard(all(pb$contribution > 0), "every playbook adds contribution")
guard(gain_to("personal_other", "contraction", "Challengers") > 0.5, "the Challengers take NGFB's personal-loan share in contractions")
guard(sum(SC$results$upside$ngfb$regimes$regime == "easing") == 8, "the upside has eight easing quarters")
guard(pbv("upside", "blended") > pbv("baseline", "blended") && pbv("baseline", "blended") > pbv("downside", "blended"),
      "playbook ordering across scenarios")
```

The positioning chapter moved NGFB's balance sheet ahead of a scenario. This
chapter asks the commercial question underneath it: in which products, and in
which phases of the cycle, does NGFB grow more slowly than its market and its
peers -- and is it worth fixing?

Two numbers place NGFB in each product and regime. The first is how fast the
**market** grows in that regime, from the sector's history (Stage 1's
territory: no bank controls it). The second is NGFB's **share effect**, how
much faster or slower than the market its book grows (Stage 2), compared with
the population of large banks it was drawn from. That population gives a
*par* (the typical large bank), a spread, and NGFB's percentile in it; only
population hyperparameters are used, never an individual bank's estimate.
NGFB's structural share drift is left out throughout, so every comparison is
about the cycle, not about trend share gains.

```{r strat-map}
#| fig-height: 6.2
#| fig-cap: "Market growth against NGFB's share effect, by macro regime. Horizontal axis: how much faster the market grows in the regime than on average; vertical axis: NGFB's growth relative to the market (percentage points a year). Bottom right: the market grows and NGFB loses share."
mp <- pos
mp$lab <- plab[mp$product]
mp$regime <- factor(rlab[mp$regime], levels = rlab)
act_lv <- c("Push", "Defend", "Guard", "Let go", "Ride", "Hold")
act_col <- c(Push = "#e34948", Defend = "#2a78d6", Guard = "#eda100", `Let go` = "#52514e",
             Ride = "#1baf7a", Hold = "#c3c2b7")
act_shp <- c(Push = 17, Defend = 15, Guard = 18, `Let go` = 25, Ride = 16, Hold = 16)
mp$action <- factor(mp$action, levels = act_lv)
ggplot(mp, aes(market_dev, ngfb_effect)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = action, fill = action, shape = action), size = 2.8) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = lab), size = 2.8, colour = ink[["primary"]], min.segment.length = 0.3,
                           segment.colour = ink[["muted"]], segment.size = 0.25, max.overlaps = Inf,
                           box.padding = 0.35, seed = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ regime, ncol = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.12)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.15)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = act_col, breaks = act_lv, name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = act_col, breaks = act_lv, name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = act_shp, breaks = act_lv, name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "market growth in the regime less its average (pp a year)",
       y = "NGFB's share effect (pp a year)") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r strat-map-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
tw <- pos[order(pos$product, pos$regime), ]
twin(data.frame(Product = plab[tw$product], Regime = rlab[tw$regime],
                `Market growth (% a year)` = num(tw$market_growth), `NGFB share effect (pp)` = sprintf("%+.2f", tw$ngfb_effect),
                `Par (pp)` = sprintf("%+.2f", tw$par), Percentile = pct(tw$percentile, 0), Action = tw$action,
                check.names = FALSE), "Table view: every product and regime")
```

The rules that turn a cell into an action are economic, not statistical. A
share **loss** in a regime where the market grows at or above its average is
under-participation: the cheapest growth NGFB forgoes, so **push**. A share
**gain** in unsecured lending while the market weakens is a warning: NGFB may
be booking the business others decline, so **guard**. Ceding unsecured share in
a contraction is the risk appetite working: **let go**. Losing share in a weak
market for a secured or funding product means competitors are taking
good-quality business: **defend**. Gains in a growing market: **ride**, with
capacity and pricing discipline.

```{r strat-playbook}
#| echo: false
pb_cells <- pos[pos$action != "Hold", ]
pb_cells <- pb_cells[order(match(pb_cells$action, c("Push", "Defend", "Guard", "Let go", "Ride")), pb_cells$product), ]
who <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(pb_cells)), function(i) {
  x <- gn[gn$product == pb_cells$product[i] & gn$regime == pb_cells$regime[i], ]
  if (!nrow(x) || pb_cells$ngfb_effect[i] >= 0) return("--")
  x <- x[order(-x$share_of_loss), ]; x <- x[x$share_of_loss >= 0.15, ]
  paste(sprintf("%s (%s)", x$to, pct(x$share_of_loss, 0)), collapse = ", ")
}, "")
kt(data.frame(Action = pb_cells$action, Product = plab[pb_cells$product], Regime = rlab[pb_cells$regime],
              `Market growth (% a year)` = num(pb_cells$market_growth),
              `NGFB vs market (pp a year)` = sprintf("%+.1f", pb_cells$ngfb_effect),
              `Typical large bank (pp)` = sprintf("%+.1f", pb_cells$par),
              Percentile = pct(pb_cells$percentile, 0), `Who gains NGFB's loss` = who,
              Why = pb_cells$rationale, check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lllrrrrll",
   caption = "The share playbook: every product and regime where NGFB should act. Who gains: the peer groups that take the share NGFB loses in that regime (proportional convention; history with NGFB embedded).")
```

**The gap is in easing cycles.** When rates fall, the card market grows
`r num(mk_g("cards", "easing"))`% a year against an average of `r num(mk_avg("cards"))`%,
yet NGFB's card book grows `r ubps(ce$ngfb_effect / 100, 0)` a year more slowly than the
market (`r pct(ce$percentile, 0)` percentile). It is not alone: the typical large bank loses
`r ubps(ce$par / 100, 0)` a year of card growth in an easing cycle too, and the
Challengers take `r pct(gain_to("cards", "easing", "Challengers"), 0)` of what NGFB loses. Corporate loans
(`r sprintf("%+.1f", co$ngfb_effect)` pp a year, `r pct(co$percentile, 0)` percentile) and vehicle and asset
finance (`r sprintf("%+.1f", ve$ngfb_effect)` pp, `r pct(ve$percentile, 0)` percentile) follow the same pattern,
in markets growing `r num(mk_g("corp_all", "easing"))`% and `r num(mk_g("vaf", "easing"))`% a year. In hiking
cycles the picture reverses: NGFB gains card share (`r sprintf("%+.1f", ch$ngfb_effect)` pp a year), so the
pattern a bank might expect -- losing cards when rates are high -- is not
NGFB's problem; losing them when rates fall is.

## Is it worth pushing?

Share is worth buying only if the extra business earns more than it costs at
the margin. The scenario engine is the wrong tool for that question: it grows
NGFB's treasury and other assets along with its loan book, which is right for
a scenario but not for a single-product decision. So each product's marginal
economics are built up directly, per rand of balance: the yield, less the
funds-transfer price (the marginal wholesale rate), less the cost of the HQLA
buffer that wholesale funding needs for its 30-day runoff, less expected
losses at the product's loss rate, after tax, less a charge for the capital
it consumes at a `r pct(CFG$cet1_target)` CET1 target and a `r pct(CFG$coe)` cost
of equity. Deposits earn the funding they displace. The BA returns carry no
costs by product, so the result is a contribution *before* operating costs:
the most it could cost to originate and service the business before it
destroys value (the headroom).

```{r strat-econ}
#| echo: false
eb <- mg[mg$scenario == "baseline" & mg$funding == "wholesale", ]
ea <- stats::aggregate(cbind(rate, ftp, liquidity, expected_loss, capital_charge, headroom) ~ product, eb, mean)
eh <- stats::aggregate(headroom ~ product, mg[mg$scenario == "baseline" & mg$funding == "blended", ], mean)
ea <- merge(ea, eh, by = "product", suffixes = c("", "_blended"), all.x = TRUE)
ea <- ea[match(names(plab), ea$product), ]
kt(data.frame(Product = plab[ea$product], `Rate (%)` = num(ea$rate, 2), `FTP (%)` = num(ea$ftp, 2),
              `Liquidity buffer` = num(ea$liquidity, 2), `Expected loss` = num(ea$expected_loss, 2),
              `Capital charge` = num(ea$capital_charge, 2),
              `Headroom, wholesale funding` = sprintf("%+.2f", ea$headroom),
              `Headroom, own deposits` = ifelse(ea$product %in% c("nmd", "beh_term"), "--", sprintf("%+.2f", ea$headroom_blended)),
              check.names = FALSE), align = "lrrrrrrr",
   caption = "Marginal economics in the baseline, percent a year of balance (three-year averages). Headroom: pre-tax contribution after funding, liquidity, expected losses, tax and the capital charge, before operating costs. 'Own deposits': the push brings matching deposits, funded at NGFB's average cost of funds.")
```

Cards clear the bar comfortably even on wholesale funding
(`r sprintf("%+.1f", hm("cards"))` pp of headroom). Corporate lending clears it only narrowly
(`r sprintf("%+.1f", hm("corp_all"))` pp) and vehicle and asset finance barely at all
(`r sprintf("%+.2f", hm("vaf"))` pp); with matching deposits both have
`r sprintf("%.1f", hm("corp_all", f = "blended"))` and `r sprintf("%.1f", hm("vaf", f = "blended"))` pp to spare. The
commercial lesson is the same for every secured product: at NGFB's margins,
lending growth pays when it brings its own funding.

```{r strat-value}
#| echo: false
vt <- val[val$action %in% c("Push", "Defend") & val$to == "par", ]
vf <- val[val$action %in% c("Push", "Defend") & val$to == "frontier", ]
vt <- merge(vt, vf[, c("product", "regime", "scenario", "funding", "contribution", "d_balance_end")],
            by = c("product", "regime", "scenario", "funding"), suffixes = c("", "_fr"))
w <- stats::reshape(vt[, c("product", "regime", "scenario", "funding", "contribution", "contribution_fr", "d_balance_end_fr")],
                    idvar = c("product", "regime", "scenario"), timevar = "funding", direction = "wide")
w <- w[order(w$product, w$regime, match(w$scenario, scen)), ]
kt(data.frame(Strategy = paste(plab[w$product], tolower(rlab[w$regime]), sep = ", "),
              Scenario = sc_short[w$scenario],
              `Extra book at the frontier (R bn)` = num(w$d_balance_end_fr.wholesale / 1e6, 1),
              `To par, wholesale (R m)` = sprintf("%+.0f", w$contribution.wholesale / 1e3),
              `To par, own deposits (R m)` = ifelse(is.na(w$contribution.blended), "--", sprintf("%+.0f", w$contribution.blended / 1e3)),
              `To the frontier, wholesale (R m)` = sprintf("%+.0f", w$contribution_fr.wholesale / 1e3),
              `To the frontier, own deposits (R m)` = ifelse(is.na(w$contribution_fr.blended), "--", sprintf("%+.0f", w$contribution_fr.blended / 1e3)),
              check.names = FALSE), align = "llrrrrr",
   caption = "What closing each gap is worth: contribution over three years, before operating costs, if NGFB's share effect in that regime moved to the typical large bank's (par) or to a top-quintile bank's (frontier). Only scenarios that contain the regime are shown.")
```

Moving every push and defend cell to par adds `r srm(pbv("baseline", "wholesale"))` to
`r srm(pbv("baseline", "blended"))` of contribution over three years in the baseline
(`r bps(pbv("baseline", "wholesale", "d_roe"), 0)` to `r bps(pbv("baseline", "blended", "d_roe"), 0)` of ROE before
operating costs), and `r srm(pbv("upside", "wholesale"))` to `r srm(pbv("upside", "blended"))` in the
upside, whose eight easing quarters are where the gaps sit. These are modest
because NGFB is a typical large bank by construction: the prize is in moving
to the frontier, where corporate lending alone is worth
`r srm(vv("corp_all", "easing", "upside", "frontier", "blended"))` in the upside if the book brings its deposits.

**Guard: cards in a contraction.** In contractions NGFB *gains* card share
(`r sprintf("%+.1f", cc$ngfb_effect)` pp a year, `r pct(cc$percentile, 0)` percentile) while the card market all
but stops (`r num(mk_g("cards", "contraction"))`% a year). At the average card loss rate the extra
book still pays -- giving it up would cost `r urm(vv("cards", "contraction", "downside"))` over the downside --
but its headroom is only `r sprintf("%.1f", mean(mg$headroom[mg$product == "cards" & mg$scenario == "downside" & mg$funding == "wholesale"]))` pp: if the
accounts won in a downturn lose more than that above the average card loss
rate, the share gain destroys value. Adverse selection in a contraction (the
customers other banks are declining) makes that likely, so the action is to
tighten underwriting on new card business when GDP turns, not to celebrate the
share. Personal loans in hiking cycles carry the same flag; in contractions
NGFB cedes personal-loan share (`r pct(pc$percentile, 0)` percentile, mostly to the
Challengers), which is the risk appetite working.

**Defend: term deposits when rates rise.** In hiking cycles the term-deposit
market grows `r num(mk_g("beh_term", "hiking"))`% a year and NGFB's share falls
(`r sprintf("%+.1f", th$ngfb_effect)` pp a year against a par of `r sprintf("%+.1f", th$par)`). Each rand of term
deposits displaces wholesale funding with `r sprintf("%.1f", hm("beh_term"))` pp of headroom, so
price-matching term deposits in a hiking cycle pays as long as gathering them
costs less than that.

::: {.callout-note}
## Caveats
The positioning comes from NGFB's drawn share parameters, which are a typical
large bank's behaviour plus a random deviation (seed 20260622); a real bank
would use its own estimates. Share effects are averages over the regime's
history, with wide uncertainty for unsecured products. Contributions exclude
operating costs and fee income, both of which the returns do not report by
product, and the frontier is a statistical construct (the 80th percentile of
the population's predictive distribution), not a named competitor.
:::

# Macro-adjusted performance: could NGFB have done better? {#performance}

```{r perf-setup}
#| include: false
sc <- PF$scorecards; vb <- PF$vs_baseline; hpar <- PF$history; rec <- PF$recent
scv <- function(s, p, col) sc[sc$scenario == s & sc$product == p, col]
vbv <- function(s, p, col) vb[vb$scenario == s & vb$product == p, col]
guard(scv("downside", "cards", "verdict") == "Near the frontier" && scv("downside", "corp_all", "percentile") > 0.65 &&
        scv("downside", "mortgages_com", "percentile") > 0.65, "downside frontier products")
guard(scv("downside", "mortgages_res", "percentile") < 0.5 && scv("upside", "mortgages_res", "percentile") > 0.5,
      "home loans: below par in the downside, above par in the upside")
guard(vbv("downside", "mortgages_res", "d_market") < 0 && vbv("downside", "mortgages_res", "d_share") > 0,
      "downside home-loan shortfall is the market")
guard(all(sc$percentile[sc$scenario == "upside" & sc$product %in% c("cards", "corp_all", "vaf", "nmd")] < 0.5),
      "upside: below par where the growth is")
guard(vbv("upside", "cards", "d_market") > 1 && vbv("upside", "cards", "d_share") < 0, "upside cards")
guard(rec$gap[rec$target == "g_personal_other"] < -1.5, "personal loans below macro par recently")
guard(all(rec$gap[rec$target %in% c("g_cards", "g_vaf", "g_nmd")] > 0.5), "cards, VAF and deposits above macro par")
guard(all(sc$verdict[sc$scenario == "downside" & sc$product %in% c("vaf", "personal_other")] == "Well below par"),
      "downside VAF and personal loans well below par")
```

A product's growth is the market's growth plus the bank's share effect. The
first part is the macro environment: Stage 1 says what the industry does in a
scenario, and no bank controls it. The second is what management controls,
and Stage 2 says what a typical large bank achieves in the same regimes. So
performance can be judged against two macro-adjusted benchmarks: **par**, the
share effect of the typical large bank, and the **frontier**, that of a
top-quintile large bank (the `r CFG$frontier_q * 100`th percentile of the population's
posterior predictive). NGFB's percentile says how much better it could have
done; the gap to the frontier says by how much. Over a scenario the
benchmarks are summed quarter by quarter along its sequence of regimes and
market growth, exactly as NGFB's own share effect is.

```{r perf-heat}
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "NGFB's share performance by scenario against the large-bank population: percentile of NGFB's share effect (blue above par, red below), labelled with the effect in percentage points a year."
hz <- sc
hz$lab <- plab[hz$product]; hz$lab <- factor(hz$lab, levels = rev(plab))
hz$scenario <- factor(sc_short[hz$scenario], levels = sc_short[scen])
ggplot(hz, aes(scenario, lab, fill = percentile)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%+.1f\n%s", round(share_effect, 1) + 0, pct(percentile, 0))), size = 3.1, lineheight = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = div_lo, mid = div_mid, high = div_hi, midpoint = 0.5, limits = c(0, 1),
                       breaks = c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1), labels = scales::percent_format(1),
                       name = "NGFB's percentile among large banks") +
  guides(fill = guide_colourbar(barwidth = grid::unit(7, "cm"), barheight = grid::unit(0.35, "cm"),
                                title.position = "top")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r perf-heat-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
twin(data.frame(Scenario = sc_short[sc$scenario], Product = plab[sc$product],
                `Market growth (% a year)` = num(sc$market_growth), `NGFB growth` = num(sc$ngfb_growth),
                `Share effect (pp)` = sprintf("%+.2f", sc$share_effect), `Par (pp)` = sprintf("%+.2f", sc$par),
                `Frontier (pp)` = sprintf("%+.2f", sc$frontier), Percentile = pct(sc$percentile, 0),
                Verdict = sc$verdict, check.names = FALSE), "Table view: scorecards")
```

**In the downside**, most of the slowdown in NGFB's books is the market's.
Home-loan growth falls `r ubps(vbv("downside", "mortgages_res", "d_growth") / 100)` a year against the
baseline, all of it market (`r sprintf("%+.2f", vbv("downside", "mortgages_res", "d_market"))` pp) -- but even so NGFB
is below par in home loans (`r pct(scv("downside", "mortgages_res", "percentile"), 0)` percentile), because a typical large
bank *gains* mortgage share in a contraction as lenders retreat to secured
credit, and NGFB gains less: in a downturn NGFB should lean into home loans,
with deposit funding (the wholesale headroom is thin). Cards are near the
frontier (`r pct(scv("downside", "cards", "percentile"), 0)` percentile,
`r sprintf("%.1f", scv("downside", "cards", "gap_to_frontier"))` pp a year short of it), with corporate loans and
commercial mortgages close behind (`r pct(scv("downside", "corp_all", "percentile"), 0)`): on share, NGFB could hardly
have done better -- and in cards that is precisely the guard case of the
previous chapter. Vehicle and asset finance and personal loans are well below
par.

**In the upside**, the growth is in cards, corporate lending and vehicle and
asset finance, and NGFB is below par in all three: in cards the market adds
`r sprintf("%+.1f", vbv("upside", "cards", "d_market"))` pp a year to growth against the baseline and NGFB's share
takes `r sprintf("%+.1f", vbv("upside", "cards", "d_share"))` pp back. The upside's message for management is to
protect share where the growth is, not to bank the tide.

```{r perf-attrib}
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-cap: "Change in NGFB's annual growth against the baseline, split into the market (macro: no bank controls it) and NGFB's share effect (management)."
ab <- rbind(data.frame(scenario = vb$scenario, product = vb$product, part = "Market (macro)", v = vb$d_market),
            data.frame(scenario = vb$scenario, product = vb$product, part = "NGFB's share", v = vb$d_share))
ab$lab <- factor(plab[ab$product], levels = rev(plab))
ab$scenario <- factor(sc_short[ab$scenario], levels = sc_short[c("upside", "downside")])
ggplot(ab, aes(v, lab, fill = part)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  facet_wrap(~ scenario) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`Market (macro)` = ink[["muted"]], `NGFB's share` = ent_col[["NGFB"]]), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "change in growth against the baseline (pp a year)", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r perf-attrib-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
twin(data.frame(Scenario = sc_short[vb$scenario], Product = plab[vb$product],
                `Change in growth (pp)` = sprintf("%+.2f", vb$d_growth), `Market (pp)` = sprintf("%+.2f", vb$d_market),
                `Share (pp)` = sprintf("%+.2f", vb$d_share), check.names = FALSE), "Table view: attribution against the baseline")
```

## Using it to set and judge targets

The same split turns into a macro-adjusted target. For product $p$ in quarter
$t$:

$$\text{target}_{p,t} = \underbrace{g^{\text{market}}_{p,t}}_{\text{realised, from the returns}} + \underbrace{\text{par}_{p}(\text{regime}_t)}_{\text{Stage 2}} + \text{ambition}_p,$$

and performance is actual growth less the target. The market term is
measured after the fact, so a bank is neither punished for a recession nor
rewarded for a boom; the par term adjusts for what a typical large bank does
in that phase of the cycle; the ambition is management's choice (for NGFB, the
gap to the frontier). Set in advance, the scorecards above become
scenario-contingent targets: in a downside, a home-loan share gain of at least
par; in an upside, no loss of card or corporate share.

```{r perf-history}
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "The industry against macro par: actual growth over four quarters against what each Stage 1 model implied from the realised macro path (simulated four quarters ahead from each quarter), selected products."
hh <- hpar[hpar$target %in% c("g_mortgages_res", "g_vaf", "g_cards", "g_personal_other", "g_corp_all", "g_nmd"), ]
hh$lab <- plab[sub("^g_", "", hh$target)]
hl <- rbind(data.frame(date = hh$date, lab = hh$lab, what = "Actual", v = hh$actual),
            data.frame(date = hh$date, lab = hh$lab, what = "Macro par", v = hh$implied))
ggplot(hl, aes(date, v, colour = what)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.55) +
  facet_wrap(~ lab, ncol = 3, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Actual = ink[["primary"]], `Macro par` = ent_col[["NGFB"]]), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "growth over four quarters (% a year)") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Over the last three years the industry beat macro par in cards
(`r sprintf("%+.1f", rec$gap[rec$target == "g_cards"])` pp a year), vehicle and asset finance and deposits, and fell
short in personal loans by `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(rec$gap[rec$target == "g_personal_other"]))` pp a year: lenders tightened
unsecured credit by more than growth, rates and unemployment alone explain.
The same comparison, run for a bank's own books, is the macro-adjusted
scorecard: it separates the tide from the swimming.

# Validation

## Back-test: would the industry models have tracked the industry?

```{r backtest}
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Skill against a no-change forecast over eight quarters, re-estimating every Stage 1 model on data to the origin and projecting it along the realised macro path. Ratio targets with the intercept correction."
ba <- BT$accuracy
ba$label <- S1$summary$label[match(ba$target, S1$summary$target)]
ba$origin_lab <- paste("From", qlab(ba$origin))
ba$sk <- pmax(ba$skill_used, -1.5)
ba$label <- factor(ba$label, levels = rev(S1$summary$label[order(match(S1$summary$family, c("volume", "credit", "pnl", "pricing")), S1$summary$target)]))
ggplot(ba, aes(sk, label, colour = origin_lab)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(pal$categorical[1:2])) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(1)) +
  labs(x = "skill vs no change (values below −150% shown at −150%)", y = NULL)
```

```{r backtest-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
fam <- stats::aggregate(cbind(skill, skill_ic) ~ family, ba, median)
twin(data.frame(Target = ba$label, Origin = qlab(ba$origin), `RMSE model` = num(ba$rmse_model, 2),
                `RMSE model + IC` = num(ba$rmse_model_ic, 2), `RMSE no change` = num(ba$rmse_naive, 2),
                Skill = pct(ba$skill, 0), `Skill + IC` = pct(ba$skill_ic, 0), check.names = FALSE))
```

The back-test asks the question a scenario tool must answer: *if the macro
path had been known*, would the models have tracked the sector? From the eve
of COVID (2019Q4) and the eve of the 2022–23 hiking cycle (2021Q4), every
Stage 1 model is re-estimated on data to the origin only and projected eight
quarters along the realised macro path. The model beats no change in
`r sum(ba$skill_used > 0)` of `r nrow(ba)` target-origins.

| Family | Median skill, no correction | Median skill, intercept correction |
|---|---|---|
| Pricing (spreads, deposit costs) | `r pct(fam$skill[fam$family == "pricing"], 0)` | `r pct(fam$skill_ic[fam$family == "pricing"], 0)` |
| Credit (credit-loss ratio) | `r pct(fam$skill[fam$family == "credit"], 0)` | `r pct(fam$skill_ic[fam$family == "credit"], 0)` |
| Fees and costs (over assets) | `r pct(fam$skill[fam$family == "pnl"], 0)` | `r pct(fam$skill_ic[fam$family == "pnl"], 0)` |
| Volumes (growth) | `r pct(fam$skill[fam$family == "volume"], 0)` | not applied |

: Back-test skill by family (two origins, eight quarters). {.striped}

The pricing and credit models carry real information; the volume models
carry a little; the fee and cost ratios are better forecast by "no change"
than by a model that mean-reverts to a 2008–2025 average the industry has
since left (non-interest revenue over assets has drifted down). The intercept
correction narrows that gap for non-interest revenue and improves the median
in every ratio family, so it is used for all ratio targets; it is not applied
to volume growth, where recent residuals are mostly noise.

## Does the engine's first year look like the industry's last year?

```{r recon}
#| echo: false
q1 <- res$baseline$sector$run$quarterly[1:4, ]
sp <- P$spnl; w4 <- sp$date %in% utils::tail(sp$date[is.finite(sp$nii)], 4)
act <- c(nii = sum(sp$nii[w4]), nir = sum(sp$nir[w4]), opex = sum(sp$opex[w4]) + sum(sp$indirect_tax[w4], na.rm = TRUE),
         imp = sum(sp$credit_losses[w4]), pbt = sum(sp$pbt[w4]))
eng <- c(nii = sum(q1$nii), nir = sum(q1$nir), opex = sum(q1$opex), imp = sum(q1$impairments), pbt = sum(q1$pbt))
ta_act <- mean(sp$total_assets[w4]); ta_eng <- mean(q1$total_assets)
kt(data.frame(Item = c("Net interest income", "Non-interest revenue", "Operating costs incl. indirect tax",
                       "Credit impairments", "Profit before tax", "Average total assets"),
              `Last four BA120 quarters, R bn` = num(c(act, ta_act) / 1e6, 0),
              `Engine, first projected year, R bn` = num(c(eng, ta_eng) / 1e6, 0),
              `Change` = spct(c(eng / act, ta_eng / ta_act) - 1, 0), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lrrr", caption = sprintf("Sector P&L: BA120 %s–%s against the engine's baseline %s–%s.",
                                     qlab(min(sp$date[w4])), qlab(max(sp$date[w4])), qlab(min(q1$date)), qlab(max(q1$date))))
```

The engine's first projected year starts four quarters after the last BA120
quarter, on a balance sheet `r spct(ta_eng / ta_act - 1, 0)` larger (BA900 grew
`r spct(sec_ta0 / P$gp$total_assets[P$gp$entity == "Sector" & P$gp$date == max(sp$date[w4])] - 1, 0)`
between the two dates). Revenue and costs scale with it, and the engine's
sector ROE in the first year, `r pct(mean(q1$roe))`, compares with
`r pct(mean(sp$roe[w4]) / 100)` on BA100's ordinary equity in the last four quarters. The
residual differences are the scenario's rate path and the intercept-corrected
ratios.

## Other checks

* **Engine arithmetic.** The balance sheet balances in every quarter of
  every run (relative error below 10⁻⁹); channel attributions reproduce the
  full-engine runs exactly in ROE and in net income; the bridges add up to the
  positioned ROE and net income (all guarded in the scripts).
* **Optimiser.** The linear prediction of the quadratic programme agrees
  with the full engine to `r ubps(max(abs(O$own - O$pred)), 2)` of ROE, the status quo
  comes out optimal under the baseline, as it must, and the step-by-step
  tables add up to each positioning's gain.
