* **Tests.** The package's unit tests cover parsing, the satellite search
  (recovering a known data-generating process, sign exclusion, convergence to
  the long run, both forms of the intercept correction), the model checks
  (Clark–West, the bounds test, the asymmetric decomposition, the peer-group
  roster), random-effects pooling, the engine (hand-computed NII, balance,
  hedge direction), liquidity factors and calibration, attribution in ROE and
  net income, the scenario library and the optimiser, including the
  $(2\alpha - \alpha^2)$ law for oversized positions.

# What didn't work {#what-didnt-work}

```{r wdw}
#| include: false
## the naive liquidity factors (fixed run-offs, generous inflows, no encumbrance)
nb <- N$engine_bs
naive_run <- c(beh_operational = 0.10, beh_savings = 0.10, beh_notice = 0.25, beh_term = 0.05,
               wholesale_other = 0.25, interbank = 0.5, reverse_repo = 0.5)
nb$runoff <- 0; nb$runoff[match(names(naive_run), nb$line)] <- naive_run
nb$hqla <- as.numeric(nb$line == "hqla")
lcr_naive <- liquidity_ratios(nb$balance, nb)[["lcr"]]
guard(lcr_naive > 3, "naive LCR claim")
pv_eq <- wc$refined_equation_ic$proj; pv_lv <- res$baseline$ngfb$proj
sav_drift <- utils::tail(pv_eq$c_savings, 1) - utils::tail(pv_lv$c_savings, 1)
guard(sav_drift > 0.5 && utils::tail(pv_eq$c_savings, 1) >= pv_eq$c_savings[1], "the equation-form correction drifts the savings cost")
## a month's interest annualised by twelve instead of by its day count
fx <- MM$panel_m[format(MM$panel_m$date, "%m") == "02" & is.finite(MM$panel_m$c_savings), ]
feb_gap <- mean(fx$c_savings * (1 - 12 * days_in_month(fx$date) / 365))
guard(feb_gap > 0.2 && feb_gap < 0.6, "February artefact size")
```

Each of these was tried, failed a check, and was replaced. They are recorded
because the failure is informative, and because a reader who tries the obvious
thing should know where it leads.

* **The intercept correction inside the equation, with the refined deposit
  models.** Adding the recent residual to the intercept compounds it through
  the autoregressive term; with deposit-cost models whose $\rho$ is close to
  one, it pushed the projected savings cost `r num(sav_drift, 2)` pp above the
  level-shift version by the end of the horizon, and kept it high while the
  repo rate fell. Applied as a level shift it tests better (see the model checks).
* **Selecting the single best specification.** Ranking thousands of
  specifications by pseudo-out-of-sample RMSE and keeping the winner
  forecasts worst of the three methods tried on genuinely new data; the BIC
  model average is kept.
* **Asymmetric pass-through everywhere.** Splitting the repo rate into hikes
  and cuts is significant in sample for several pricing models but improves
  both forecast tests only for savings deposits and card yields; elsewhere
  the trending partial sums make projections drift.
* **A product-level composition draw for NGFB.** Drawing all
  `r length(ngfb_asset_lines())` asset shares from six banks needs a covariance
  of dimension `r length(ngfb_asset_lines()) - 1` in log-ratio space,
  `r choose(length(ngfb_asset_lines()), 2)` parameters from six observations,
  and produced implausible books. Drawing five business-line dimensions and
  splitting within lines at the population mix fixed it.
* **Carving NGFB out of existing banks.** Taking NGFB's book from the reported
  banks distorted every peer group's history and share dynamics. Adding NGFB
  to the industry (Post 1's convention) leaves the data untouched.
* **COVID dummies on the credit-loss model.** They absorbed the 2020 stress
  signal, leaving a credit model that did not respond to a recession. The
  dummies now apply to volume models only.
* **The SARB coincident indicator as the activity measure for regimes.** It ran
  negative through 2025–26 while GDP grew, labelling an expansion a
  contraction. Regimes use real GDP only.
* **Unemployment in the credit-loss model.** No specification containing it
  survives the sign and $t$-tests once GDP is available, so the engine has no
  unemployment channel. A labour-market stress therefore shows up only
  through its GDP counterpart.
* **Macro models for mortgage growth.** None beats the AR(1) out of sample
  (skill `r pct(s1$skill[s1$target == "g_mortgages_res"], 0)`); mortgage
  volumes are close to a slow-moving trend.
* **A mean-reverting fee model.** Without the intercept correction,
  non-interest revenue over assets reverts towards its 2008–2025 average
  (`r pct(mean(SC$no_ic$nir_assets) / 100, 2)` of assets in the baseline, against
  `r pct(mean(SC$no_ic$nir_assets_ic) / 100, 2)` with it) and lifts the
  industry's baseline ROE by `r ubps(nir_gap)`. The back-test showed the same
  failure (the model lost to "no change" from both origins).
* **A single NII-matching wholesale spread, with outliers left in.** One
  quarter of BA120 call-deposit cost at `r num(cc_val, 1)`% pushed the solved
  spread to JIBAR `r sprintf("%+.2f", N$calibration$wholesale_spread_raw)` pp, an
  implausible negative funding spread. Neutralising flagged outliers gives
  JIBAR `r sprintf("%+.2f", N$calibration$wholesale_spread)` pp.
* **Calibrating gross interest flows away.** Two alternatives were tried and
  dropped: uniform level shifts on all yields and costs (which mis-state every
  product's BA120 yield), and interest-bearing shares on treasury and
  wholesale lines (which, applied to NGFB's larger treasury book, made it look
  liability-sensitive and implausibly unprofitable). Reporting the gross
  excess and matching NII was the more honest choice.
* **Naive LCR run-off factors.** Fixed run-off rates by behavioural line,
  generous inflow rates and no encumbrance put NGFB's LCR at
  `r formatC(100 * lcr_naive, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")`%. Depositor-weighted Basel factors, calibrated to the
  published sector ratio, bring it to `r pct(q0$lcr[1], 0)`.
* **Maximising the engine's ROE directly.** Without the implied marginal
  costs the optimiser puts `r raw_up` of the six lending moves at their upper bound and promises
  `r ubps(raw_gain)` of probability-weighted ROE, because the engine prices new
  volume at average economics. The reverse-optimisation step replaced it.
* **Post 2's composition weights.** Post 2 loaded a stale draw; the canonical
  Post 1 composition is used here (see the note in the NGFB section).
* **Monthly interest annualised by twelve.** A month's interest times twelve
  reads every February, with 28 days of interest, as a fall in savings-deposit
  costs of about `r num(feb_gap, 2)` pp, and every 31-day month as a small rise.
  Annualising with the month's own day count removes the artefact.
* **Monthly satellites in production.** On the same quarterly outcomes they
  forecast pricing and most volumes less accurately than the quarterly models
  (see [Monthly frequency](#monthly)); the corporate-loan and term-deposit gains
  come from the timing of large flows, which is a nowcasting point rather
  than a reason to change the scenario models.
* **Polynomial distributed lags and Bayesian shrinkage for pricing.** Both lost
  to the sign-restricted ARDL average at both frequencies: a smooth Almon lag
  profile cannot represent a repricing step at an MPC meeting, and shrinkage
  keeps many small, often wrong-signed coefficients.

# Limitations

* **Public data only.** Prices, losses and costs are the sector's; NGFB's
  differ from the sector only through its mix (and its hedge). A real bank
  would replace the Stage 1 pricing with its own product pricing and the
  relative loss multipliers with its own loss history.
* **The level of ROE rests on two modelling choices.** The deposit-cost
  dynamics moved the baseline by `r ubps(wc$previous$summary$roe - base$ngfb)` between this version
  and the last, and the intercept correction on credit losses is worth
  `r ubps(mr["baseline", "core"] - mr["baseline", "no_ic_credit"])`. The scenario differences and the positioning
  are much less sensitive to either.
* **Relative loss multipliers are assumptions.** BA200 publishes no losses by
  product, so the ordering (unsecured highest, mortgages lowest) is an
  external calibration normalised to the sector's credit-loss ratio.
* **Volumes are the weakest link.** The volume models beat a naive benchmark
  only modestly, and the share models' regime effects are imprecise. Scenario
  ROE is driven far more by pricing and credit, which are better identified.
* **The sector is unhedged in the engine.** Real banks hedge; the sector line
  shows the industry's gross macro exposure, not its reported earnings
  sensitivity.
* **NGFB's hedge is not re-optimised for the refined deposit models.** The
  canonical 49.6% ratio comes from Post 3; with faster deposit repricing it now
  over-hedges, which is a finding about the canonical bank, not a
  recommendation for a real one.
* **Execution costs size the moves.** Their direction is robust; their
  magnitude scales with an assumption about how expensive it is to move a
  franchise inside a year.
* **No second-round feedback.** The scenarios are exogenous: NGFB's actions do
  not move prices or the macro path, and the sector does not respond to NGFB.
* **Liquidity proxies.** BA900 cannot see the 30-day maturity slice,
  operational status, committed facilities or derivatives; one scalar per
  ratio calibrates the level to the Prudential Authority's published figures.
* **Monthly data.** `r if (MM$vol_source == "KBP") "Until the monthly BA900 pull has run, the monthly volume comparison uses the SARB's credit statistics (all monetary institutions), whose product definitions differ from BA900's, and the monthly sector balance sheet is interpolated between quarter ends." else "Month-end BA900 balances carry window dressing and lumpy wholesale flows that quarterly data average out; the month-of-year dummies absorb only the regular part, and monthly and quarterly ratios differ slightly in definition when balances move within a quarter."`
  Unemployment and house prices have no monthly indicator here, so their
  monthly paths are smooth, and the monthly GDP path is only as good as its
  three indicators.
* **Share strategy and scorecards rest on NGFB's drawn share parameters.**
  They are a typical large bank's behaviour plus a random deviation; a real
  bank would use its own estimates, which would be noisier for small books.
  Contributions exclude operating costs and fees, which the returns do not
  report by product, and assume marginal growth is funded at the wholesale
  rate unless it brings its own deposits.
* **The local projections are not identified.** Without measured
  monetary-policy shocks, they show how rates and credit move together, not
  the causal effect of a rate change on lending.

# Reproducing the analysis {#reproducing-the-analysis}

The code is an R package, `baeconstrat`, with the analysis in separate
scripts.

```text
BA-econ-strat/
├── DESCRIPTION, NAMESPACE, LICENSE, README.md
├── R/                      package functions (documented, exported)
├── data-raw/               pull scripts and the downloaded caches
├── analysis/               00_config.R … 11_performance.R, run_all.R
├── inst/artefacts/         NGFB canonical constants and composition draw
├── tests/testthat/         unit tests
├── output/                 *.rds written by the analysis scripts
└── report/                 this document
```

```r
# from the package root, after the data pull (data-raw/00_pull_data.bat, and
# data-raw/03_pull_monthly.bat for the monthly BA900 and BA100 returns)
install.packages(".", repos = NULL, type = "source")
source("analysis/run_all.R")
quarto::quarto_render("report/ngfb_macro_strategy.qmd")
```

Settings live in `analysis/00_config.R` (jump-off, horizon, baseline paths,
floors, scenario probabilities, the form of the intercept correction). The
model-check script fails if the Stage 1 registry disagrees with its own
adoption rules. The seed is `r CFG$seed`. Every number in this report is
computed inline from `output/*.rds`; `guard()` stops the render if an input
drifts from what the text says.
